zonal-atlantic-flow.name: Zonal Atlantic westerly flow

monthNotes.jan: Peak season: mild, wet and windy; frequent named storms when the jet is strong.
monthNotes.jun: In summer the same pattern means cool, cloudy, showery weather rather than storms.
monthNotes.jul: A "washout" summer pattern when it persists.
monthNotes.oct: The classic autumn return of the Atlantic.

zonal-atlantic-flow.summary: The jet stream runs more or less straight from west to east across or near the UK, sending a procession of Atlantic lows and fronts across the country with brief ridges of high pressure between them.
body: This is the UK's default circulation, especially from autumn to early spring. Low pressure near Iceland and high pressure near the Azores drive a westerly or south-westerly flow; in winter the Met Office describes this as the positive phase of the North Atlantic Oscillation, which strengthens the westerlies and brings milder maritime air, more rain and more wind storms.

What it delivers depends on season and on exactly where the jet sits. With the jet over the UK, fronts cross every day or two; with it to the north, the south gets drier ridges while Scotland stays wet; with it further south, England and Wales take the brunt. In summer the same pattern gives changeable, cool, cloudy days rather than storms.
regions: Moist westerly air is forced up the western hills: the wettest, windiest conditions.
In the rain shadow of western hills: drier, often brighter between fronts.
Sheltered by the Pennines but exposed to strong westerly gusts.

essential: A strong, fairly straight (zonal) jet stream across the North Atlantic.
A pressure gradient between low pressure to the north-west and high pressure to the south.
favourable: A large north–south temperature contrast over North America and the Atlantic, which strengthens the jet.
No blocking high over Scandinavia or Greenland to divert the lows.
setup.pressure: Low to the north and north-west of the UK, high to the south (Azores).
setup.airmass: Polar maritime and tropical maritime air, alternating behind and ahead of fronts.
setup.jet: Across or just north of the UK, flowing west to east.
setup.fronts: Frequent warm, cold and occluded fronts.
setup.orography: Rain is greatly enhanced on western, windward hills and suppressed in their lee.

outcomes: Alternating rain belts and showery, brighter interludes.
Mild temperatures for the time of year, especially by night in winter.
Strong winds and gales, particularly in the north and west.
Large west–east rainfall contrasts: very wet western uplands, drier east.
zonal-atlantic-flow.alternatives: If the jet weakens or buckles, this can switch to a blocked pattern within days. If the jet is unusually strong, it can turn stormy, with deep lows (see Strong, fast Atlantic jet stream).
zonal-atlantic-flow.duration: Spells of days to weeks; whole winters can be dominated by it.

impacts.transport: Ferry cancellations in the west, wind-related road and rail restrictions.
impacts.rivers: Repeated rain raises western rivers and saturates soils.

signals: Pressure charts and the North Atlantic Oscillation index
A deep Icelandic low and strong Azores high signal westerlies.
The index summarises a pattern; it does not forecast individual storms.
Jet-stream wind charts at about 250–300 hPa
Show where lows will be steered and deepen.
Small shifts in jet position change which regions get the rain.
Ensemble forecasts
Agreement on a zonal pattern is often good several days ahead.
Timing of individual fronts is less certain beyond about three days.
zonal-atlantic-flow.frequency: A seasonally common pattern in autumn and winter; it occurs in summer too but usually less persistently.

climate.observed: Year-to-year variations in the winter westerlies are large, and natural variability dominates the record.
climate.projected: UK climate projections indicate wetter winters on average; how storm tracks themselves will change is less certain.
climate.uncertainty: Changes in the jet stream and North Atlantic Oscillation are an active research area with competing influences.

strong-jet-stream.name: Strong, fast Atlantic jet stream

monthNotes.feb: February 2022 (Dudley, Eunice, Franklin) and February 2020 (Ciara, Dennis) were both jet-driven stormy spells.
monthNotes.aug: Unusual in summer but possible: storms Ellen and Francis (August 2020) were jet-driven.

strong-jet-stream.summary: An unusually strong jet stream over or near the UK both steers lows towards the country and helps them deepen, producing a run of storms and heavy rain.
body: The jet stream exists because of the temperature contrast between polar and tropical air, so it is strongest in winter. When an exceptionally cold air mass over North America meets mild air further south, the contrast — and the jet — can intensify further; the Met Office linked storms Isha and Jocelyn (January 2024) to exactly this.

A strong jet acts, in the Met Office's words, a bit like a vacuum cleaner, removing air from the top of a developing low so that its central pressure falls. Lows forming on the jet can deepen quickly and race across the UK, one after another, every day or two.
regions: Most often closest to the low centres.
Heavy orographic rain on each frontal passage.
Takes the brunt when the jet dips south.

essential: A jet core of unusually high speed across the Atlantic towards the UK.
A large thermal contrast across the jet.
favourable: Cold air outbreaks over North America.
A flat (zonal) jet that does not buckle.
Lows forming near the jet exit or entrance regions where air is removed aloft.
setup.jet: Strong, straight jet aimed at the British Isles.
setup.pressure: Deep Atlantic lows, often several in sequence.

outcomes: A succession of named storms with gales or severe gales.
Repeated heavy rain on saturated ground, escalating flood risk.
Mild, blustery conditions; snow mainly on northern hills behind cold fronts.
strong-jet-stream.alternatives: The same strong jet slightly further north keeps storms over Iceland and Scotland and leaves the south mild and fairly dry.
strong-jet-stream.duration: Typically one to three weeks; exceptionally longer (December 2013 to February 2014).

impacts.people: Danger from falling trees and debris; coastal waves.
impacts.transport: Repeated travel disruption over successive storms.
impacts.power: Repeated outages; repairs hampered by the next storm.
impacts.rivers: Cumulative flooding as catchments stay full.

signals: Jet-stream charts
A jet core well above normal speed aimed at the UK.
Speed alone does not tell you where lows will deepen.
Ensemble spread in pressure
Run-to-run consistency in a stormy regime is often good even when individual storm details are not.
Exact track and depth of each low remain uncertain until 1–3 days ahead.
strong-jet-stream.frequency: A recurrent feature of many winters; most likely December to February.

climate.observed: Stormy winters have occurred throughout the record; there is no simple trend in UK storminess.
climate.projected: Some projections suggest a modest strengthening and eastward extension of the winter jet, but this is uncertain.

events.title: Early winter storms, late 2011
events.summary: A powerful jet stream sent a succession of deep depressions across the north. The 8 December storm was the most significant for Scotland since January 2005.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots widely in Scotland; mountain summits well over 100 knots (115 mph).

events.title: Winter storms, December 2013 to February 2014
events.summary: A succession of at least 12 major winter storms from mid-December to mid-February: the stormiest period the UK had experienced for at least 20 years. The 5 December storm drove a major North Sea surge. As rain accumulated, concern shifted from wind to flooding — the Somerset Levels were under water for much of the winter and the Thames flooded through Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Surrey. On 5 February the railway at Dawlish was left suspended when its foundations were washed away.
observations: 5 December 2013 surge: 2 m above predicted high water, coinciding with high tide.
Around 6 major storms from late January to mid-February, 2 to 3 days apart.

events.title: Storms Ali and Bronagh
events.summary: A powerful jet stream drove two storms that marked an emphatic transition from the fine summer of 2018 to autumn. Ali was one of the most notable storms at that time of year in recent decades.
observations: Ali: gusts widely over 60 knots (69 mph) across the north.
Bronagh: well over 50 mm of rain on upland Wales and the south Pennines.

events.title: Storms Ellen and Francis
events.summary: A strong jet stream drove deep lows across the UK in late August: two of the most notable August storms of the last 50 years. Trees in full leaf on saturated ground came down; beach huts at Woolacombe were washed away.
observations: 69 knots (79 mph) at Capel Curig (Ellen); 70 knots (81 mph) at Needles Old Battery (Francis).

events.title: Storms Dudley, Eunice and Franklin
events.summary: Three named storms in a week, the first time since naming began in 2015/16. Eunice brought two rare red warnings and was the most severe and damaging storm to affect England and Wales since February 2014. Four people died in the UK and Ireland from falling trees and over a million homes lost power.
observations: Gust of 106 knots (122 mph) at Needles Old Battery, Isle of Wight — a new England gust record.
Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) widely across southern England.
Severe coastal flooding in the Severn Estuary avoided: the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in places.

events.title: Storms Isha and Jocelyn
events.summary: Two storms in quick succession driven by a powerful jet stream, itself intensified by a large temperature contrast across North America. Isha brought an amber warning over more than half the UK and an overnight red warning for north-east Scotland.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) in Northumberland.
Most significant widespread wind storm since Eunice in February 2022.

events.title: Storm Éowyn
events.summary: The UK's most powerful wind storm for over a decade and, for Northern Ireland, the most significant since the Boxing Day Storm of 1998. A red warning covered all of Northern Ireland and Scotland's Central Belt; the public were advised to stay at home and schools closed.
observations: Highest gust 87 knots (100 mph) at Drumalbin, Lanarkshire.
Tiree recorded the UK's lowest pressure since storm naming began in autumn 2015.

sourceRecords.title: Storms Isha and Jocelyn, 21 to 24 January 2024

amplified-jet.name: Slow-moving, amplified (meandering) jet stream
amplified-jet.summary: Instead of flowing straight, the jet loops north and south in large waves that move slowly. Weather systems stall, so whatever the UK has — heat, cold, rain or drought — tends to persist.
body: The Met Office compares a buckled jet to a meandering river: movement slows and lows move less predictably. Ridges in the jet carry warm air north and build high pressure; troughs carry cold air south and hold low pressure in place.

Whether this is good or bad weather for the UK depends on where the loops sit. Under a ridge the UK can be warm and dry for weeks; under a trough it can be cool and wet; on the boundary between the two, slow-moving fronts can bring exceptional rainfall.
regions: The outcome depends entirely on where the ridges and troughs sit relative to the UK.

essential: Large-amplitude waves in the jet stream.
Slow eastward progression of those waves.
favourable: A weaker jet (smaller temperature contrast), more typical in spring and summer.
Blocking highs that help hold the pattern.

outcomes: Long dry, settled spells under ridges.
Persistent cool, showery or wet spells under troughs.
Slow-moving fronts with prolonged heavy rain on the boundaries.
Unusual wind directions (northerly, easterly, southerly) rather than westerly.
amplified-jet.alternatives: A small shift in the wave pattern can turn a hot ridge into a thundery trough within a day or two.
amplified-jet.duration: Often a week or more; can recur for a whole season.

impacts.agriculture: Persistent anomalies — too dry or too wet — affect crops more than short spells.
impacts.rivers: Either drought or prolonged high flows, depending on position.

signals: Upper-air (500 hPa) height charts
Large ridges and troughs over the Atlantic and Europe.
Forecast skill for the exact position of slow waves can drop sharply beyond about 5 days.
Ensembles
Clustering of members into different ridge/trough positions shows how uncertain the outcome is.
Ensembles can be over-confident about blocks breaking down too quickly.
amplified-jet.frequency: Plausible in any month; amplified patterns and blocking are noted by the Met Office as most common in spring.

climate.observed: Whether the jet is becoming wavier is debated.
climate.projected: Some research links Arctic warming to a wavier jet; other work finds competing effects.
climate.uncertainty: The Met Office describes the relative importance of competing effects as uncertain and an area of active research.

jet-north.name: Jet stream unusually far north

monthNotes.jul: In summer the jet usually lies north of the UK anyway; when it sits well north for weeks, summers like 2018 result.
monthNotes.jan: In winter, a northern jet gives mild, often dry weather in the south while Scotland stays wet and windy.

jet-north.summary: With the jet stream displaced north of the UK, Atlantic lows track towards Iceland and Norway while high pressure covers much of the country — especially the south.
body: The Met Office notes that in summer the jet usually lies to the north of the UK, allowing high pressure to bring calmer, drier weather; a jet held unusually far north extends and intensifies that. Heatwaves are most common when high pressure develops in this way.
In winter the same displacement keeps England and Wales mild and fairly dry under the Azores high, while northern Scotland may still catch fronts and gales.
regions: Most often under the high: dry, sunny, warm in summer.
Still near the storm track: wetter and windier.

essential: Jet stream displaced north of its usual latitude for the season.
favourable: Warm, dry soils in summer that reinforce heat.
setup.pressure: High pressure over or south of the UK.

outcomes: Long dry spells, especially in the south and east.
Heat in summer; mild, quiet weather in winter.
A north–south split: rain and wind confined to the far north-west.
jet-north.alternatives: If the high sits to the east, hot southerly plumes and thunderstorms become possible.

impacts.agriculture: Drying soils in spring and summer.
impacts.rivers: Falling river levels in the south.

signals: Jet and 500 hPa height charts
Persistent ridge over the UK and jet over Iceland.
The block can break down faster or slower than forecast.
jet-north.frequency: Seasonally common in high summer; plausible in other months.

climate.observed: Summer 2018 was associated with this kind of pattern.
climate.projected: UK projections indicate hotter, drier summers on average, consistent with more frequent settled spells, though circulation changes are uncertain.

regionRows.reason: Most often under the high: dry, sunny, warm in summer.
Most often under the high: dry, sunny, warm in summer.

events.title: Summer 2018
events.summary: High pressure dominated June and July: the warmest UK summer since 2006, the driest since 2003 and the sunniest since 1995.
observations: A run of over 50 dry days at some south-eastern stations, lasting until late July.
30 °C exceeded fairly widely on 15 days.
A Met Office study found a summer this hot is about 30 times more likely now than before the industrial revolution.

jet-south.name: Jet stream unusually far south

monthNotes.jun: In summer this means lows tracking across southern Britain: the pattern behind the record wet April–July 2012 and summer 2007.
monthNotes.jan: In winter, lows track to the south and cold air can sit to the north: the battleground for snow.

jet-south.summary: With the jet stream pushed south of the UK, Atlantic lows track across southern Britain or France instead of near Iceland. In summer that means cool, wet weather; in winter it can bring cold air in from the north or east.
body: The Met Office attributed the record rainfall of April to July 2012 to a shift of the jet stream to a much more southerly track than normal, bringing a succession of Atlantic lows and fronts across the southern half of the UK — while the far north-west of Scotland stayed unusually dry.

In winter a southern jet often goes with high pressure to the north (a negative North Atlantic Oscillation). Cold air from the north or east can then reach the UK while lows run along the Channel, and where the two meet heavy snow is possible.
regions: Frontal rain enhanced on the hills.
Often under higher pressure: drier than normal.

essential: Jet stream south of its usual position for the season.
favourable: Blocking high pressure over Greenland or Scandinavia.
setup.jet: Over France or the Bay of Biscay.

outcomes: Persistent rain and showers over southern Britain.
Cool, cloudy summers with flood risk.
In winter: cold northerly or easterly air with snow chances, especially where fronts meet cold air.
jet-south.alternatives: The far north can be drier and sunnier than the south — the reverse of the usual pattern.
jet-south.duration: Weeks to months in the most persistent cases.

impacts.rivers: Prolonged high flows and flooding in southern and central catchments.
impacts.transport: In winter, snow and ice disruption on the boundary with cold air.

signals: Jet-stream and pressure-anomaly charts
A persistent southern storm track and high pressure to the north.
Persistence is hard to forecast beyond a couple of weeks.
jet-south.frequency: Plausible in any month; it is the pattern behind several of the wettest UK summers on record.

regionRows.reason: Frontal rain enhanced on the hills.
Often under higher pressure: drier than normal.
Often under higher pressure: drier than normal.

events.title: Summer 2007 floods
events.summary: Record June and July rainfall: heavy rain on 24–25 June over Yorkshire and the Humber and on 19–20 July over the south Midlands brought widespread flooding and transport disruption.
observations: July 2007: over twice the average rainfall over large areas of England and Wales, over four times locally in the south Midlands.
Return period of the high totals estimated at over 200 years (Met Office).

events.title: Record rainfall, April to July 2012
events.summary: A shift of the jet stream to a much more southerly track than normal sent a succession of lows across the southern half of the UK, abruptly ending the 2010–2012 drought. The far north-west of Scotland stayed much drier than average.
observations: April, June and April–July each the wettest on record in the England & Wales series from 1766.
Summer 2012 the wettest for the UK since 1912.

blocking-high.name: Blocking high pressure

monthNotes.apr: The Met Office notes blocks are most common in spring.
monthNotes.jul: A summer block can mean a long heatwave and drought (1976).
monthNotes.jan: A winter block can mean weeks of cold (1963) or of grey, still gloom, depending on where it sits.

blocking-high.summary: A large area of high pressure stays nearly stationary and diverts the usual west-to-east procession of weather systems around it, sometimes for weeks.
body: The Met Office describes two main types. In an omega block a high is sandwiched between two lows, the pattern looking like the Greek letter Ω; in a diffluent block the jet splits around a high. Blocks are most common in spring but can persist for months exceptionally — around mid-summer in 1976 and mid-winter in 1963.

Under the high it stays mainly dry and settled; on its edges fronts can stall and give prolonged rain. What the UK feels depends on where the block sits: over the UK it brings dry, light-wind weather; to the north or east it can drive cold easterlies; to the west it can bring northerlies.
regions: Everywhere can be affected; the position of the block decides who gets the dry weather and who gets the stalled fronts.

essential: A slow-moving or stationary high-pressure system.
A weak or diverted jet stream.
favourable: A sudden stratospheric warming (winter), which can make blocking more likely in following weeks.
setup.pressure: A persistent high, often with lows on either side.

outcomes: In summer: heat, sunshine and drought development.
In winter: frost, fog, cold easterlies — or mild, cloudy gloom.
Stalled fronts and heavy rain on the edge of the block.
blocking-high.alternatives: The same block can bring opposite weather to different parts of the UK.
blocking-high.duration: Several days to several weeks; exceptionally months.

impacts.agriculture: Drought in summer; prolonged frost in winter.
impacts.people: Heat-health risks in summer; cold-health risks in winter.

signals: 500 hPa height and pressure charts
A closed high or ridge that ensembles keep in place.
Models have historically tended to break blocks down too quickly.
blocking-high.frequency: Plausible in every month; most common in spring.

climate.observed: Blocking frequency varies strongly between years and decades.
climate.projected: How climate change will alter blocking near the UK is uncertain.

events.title: Winter of 1962–63
events.summary: A high north-east of the British Isles from 22 December dragged bitterly cold winds across the country for most of the winter — the coldest in England and Wales since 1740. Snow covered much of England every day until early March; even sea water froze in some harbours.
observations: Braemar −22.2 °C on 18 January 1963.
Blizzard of 29–30 December with drifts up to 6 m in Wales and south-west England.

events.title: Spring 2025
events.summary: High pressure building from the Azores or the continent dominated, blocking Atlantic fronts. The UK's warmest, sunniest and sixth-driest spring on record — sunnier than all but three historical summers.
observations: A large positive pressure anomaly between Scotland and Norway, particularly in April.

greenland-block.name: Greenland blocking

monthNotes.dec: December 2010 had strong high-latitude blocking with persistent cold.
monthNotes.jun: In summer a Greenland high pushes the jet south: cool, unsettled weather rather than cold.

greenland-block.summary: High pressure over or near Greenland diverts the jet stream south. The UK loses its mild westerlies and draws air from the north instead, with lows passing to the south.
body: This is a strongly negative North Atlantic Oscillation. The Met Office explains that when pressure is higher than usual over Iceland and lower than usual over the Azores, more of the UK's weather comes from the north or east — in winter meaning colder, drier and potentially snowy conditions.

Arctic maritime air can flood south on northerly winds, bringing snow showers to northern and eastern coasts. If an Atlantic low then runs into the cold air from the south-west, a band of heavy snow can form along its northern edge.
regions: First to receive Arctic air and snow showers.
Snow showers in northerly and north-easterly winds.
Lows tracking along the Channel can bring frontal snow or heavy rain.

essential: A persistent high over Greenland or Iceland.
Jet displaced south of the UK.
favourable: A weakened stratospheric polar vortex, which typically favours a negative North Atlantic Oscillation.

outcomes: Cold northerly spells with snow showers.
Frontal snow where Atlantic lows meet the cold air.
greenland-block.alternatives: In summer a Greenland high gives cool, wet weather rather than cold.
greenland-block.duration: Often a week or two; occasionally most of a winter.

impacts.transport: Snow and ice disruption.
impacts.people: Cold-health risks.

signals: North Atlantic Oscillation forecasts
A forecast negative NAO raises the chance of cold northerly or easterly spells.
NAO forecasts carry limited skill beyond a couple of weeks.
Stratospheric polar vortex monitoring
A weak vortex can precede blocking.
The Met Office stresses that a stratospheric warming does not always affect UK weather.
greenland-block.frequency: Plausible in winter and spring; uncommon as a cold driver in summer.

scandinavian-block.name: Scandinavian blocking high

monthNotes.feb: The classic driver of severe cold: 1947, 2018 ("Beast from the East") and February 2021.
monthNotes.oct: In autumn a Scandinavian block held Storm Babet in place, giving extreme rain in eastern Scotland.
monthNotes.apr: In spring the same block brought the UK its warmest, sunniest spring on record in 2025.

scandinavian-block.summary: A large high over Scandinavia blocks Atlantic weather and turns the UK's winds easterly or south-easterly. In winter this can mean bitter cold and snow; in spring and summer, dry and sunny weather; in autumn, stalled rain-bearing fronts.
body: The Met Office case study of 1947 describes high pressure moving over southern Scandinavia and setting up a pattern that dominated the UK for weeks. A sudden stratospheric warming can make such blocks more likely: the Met Office notes that the resulting blocking typically forms over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia, with cold easterlies developing on its southern flank.

The same block brings very different weather by season. In winter the easterly wind carries continental cold, and picks up moisture over the North Sea to form snow showers. In spring it gives dry, sunny, cool-breezed weather. In autumn, Storm Babet (2023) was held in place by a Scandinavian block, so its rain fell on the same areas of eastern Scotland for many hours.
regions: Exposed to North Sea-modified easterly air: snow showers in winter, haar and cloud in spring and summer.
Close to the continent: coldest or warmest air arrives here first.
Sheltered from easterly showers; often the sunniest areas in this pattern.

essential: High pressure centred over Scandinavia or the North Sea.
An easterly or south-easterly flow across the UK.
favourable: Relatively warm North Sea (adds moisture for snow showers).

outcomes: Winter: bitterly cold easterlies, North Sea snow showers, ice days.
Spring/summer: dry, sunny west; cool, cloudy east coasts.
Autumn: fronts stalled against the block, prolonged rain.
scandinavian-block.alternatives: If the high sits further south, the UK may stay in a light south-easterly with fog and frost rather than snow.

impacts.transport: Severe disruption in snowy winter outbreaks.
impacts.people: Wind-chill and cold-health risks.

signals: Pressure and 850 hPa temperature charts
A Scandinavian high with very cold air (−10 °C or lower at 850 hPa) advecting west signals a severe cold spell.
Small changes in the high's position decide whether the cold arrives.
Sudden stratospheric warming monitoring
Can give weeks of warning of an increased chance of blocking.
Not every warming leads to UK cold.
scandinavian-block.frequency: Plausible in every month; most common in spring.

events.title: Winter of 1947 and the March snowmelt floods
events.summary: High pressure over southern Scandinavia set up a pattern that dominated for weeks. Snow fell somewhere in the UK every day for 55 days. When milder air and Atlantic rain arrived in mid-March, meltwater ran off ground still frozen solid, and rivers across England burst their banks; 70% of houses in Selby were flooded.
observations: Drifts up to seven metres deep in Scotland by 12 March.
Woburn fell to −21 °C on 25 February.
Snow depth of 1.65 m near Ruthin in March 1947 — the deepest recorded in an inhabited area of the UK.

events.title: Storm Babet
events.summary: A blocking high over Scandinavia held the system in place, bringing exceptional rain to eastern Scotland (two red warnings for rain) and heavy, widespread rain across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
observations: 150 to 200 mm in the wettest parts of eastern Scotland.
For Angus, 19 October 2023 was by a wide margin the wettest day in a series from 1891.
The Midlands provisionally recorded its wettest 3-day period on record.

events.title: Spring 2025
events.summary: High pressure building from the Azores or the continent dominated, blocking Atlantic fronts. The UK's warmest, sunniest and sixth-driest spring on record — sunnier than all but three historical summers.
observations: A large positive pressure anomaly between Scotland and Norway, particularly in April.

azores-high.name: Azores high ridging over the UK
aka: ridge of high pressure from the south-west
azores-high.summary: The semi-permanent high near the Azores extends a ridge north-east over the UK, giving settled, often fine weather — especially in the south.
body: The Azores high is the southern half of the pressure pattern that drives the UK's westerlies. When it ridges north-east, fronts are pushed towards Scotland and Scandinavia. Spring 2025, the UK's sunniest on record, was dominated by high pressure building from the Azores or continental Europe.

Air under an Azores ridge has usually travelled over the ocean, so it is rarely extremely hot: expect warm sunshine in summer rather than the extreme heat of a continental plume. In winter it can mean mild, grey, drizzly days in the west and frost or fog under clearer skies in the east.
regions: Closest to the ridge; most settled.
Fronts can still reach the far north.

essential: A ridge of the Azores high extending over or near the UK.

outcomes: Dry, settled weather in the south and west.
Pleasant warmth in summer; mild cloudy days or frosty nights in winter.
Fronts weakening as they reach the north-west.
azores-high.duration: Days to a couple of weeks.

impacts.agriculture: Good working weather; drying soils if prolonged.

signals: Pressure charts
Isobars curving anticyclonically from the Azores to the UK.
Ridges often weaken faster than models suggest.
azores-high.frequency: Seasonally common in late spring and summer; plausible in other months.

deep-atlantic-low.name: Deep Atlantic depression

monthNotes.apr: April storms do occur (Hannah 2019, Noa 2023, Kathleen 2024, Dave 2026) and trees coming into leaf make them more damaging.
monthNotes.aug: Summer storms are unusual but August 2020 had two (Ellen and Francis).

deep-atlantic-low.summary: A large, intense area of low pressure tracks in from the Atlantic, bringing gales or severe gales, heavy rain and large waves, usually followed by squally showers.
body: Deep lows form where warm and cold air meet beneath the jet stream. The Met Office notes that, in general, the lower the central pressure the stronger the winds. As the system passes, the warm front brings rain, the warm sector mild drizzly air, the cold front a narrow band of heavy rain and a wind change, and the cold air behind it gusty showers, with snow on northern hills in winter.

Many deep lows are "fairly typical winter storms — notable but not exceptional", as the Met Office wrote of Storm Erik (2019). Their impact depends heavily on track, timing and season: trees in full leaf in early autumn or late spring are more vulnerable, and a storm arriving with high spring tides can bring coastal flooding.
regions: Exposed coasts and headlands record the strongest gusts.
Most often closest to the low centres.
Storms tracking further south bring severe gusts to the south coast (Needles Old Battery often records the highest).

essential: A developing extratropical cyclone with a large pressure gradient.
A jet stream to support deepening.
favourable: Warm, moist air feeding the warm sector.
setup.pressure: Central pressure often below 970 hPa; exceptionally below 950 hPa.

outcomes: Gales or severe gales; damaging gusts on exposed coasts and hills.
Heavy rain, especially on western uplands.
Large waves and spray on exposed coasts.
Squally showers, hail and thunder behind the cold front; hill snow in winter.
deep-atlantic-low.alternatives: A low that passes north of Scotland may give the south only a breezy, wet day; one that tracks across England can bring the strongest winds south of its centre.
deep-atlantic-low.duration: Typically 12 to 36 hours of impacts per storm.

impacts.people: Falling trees and debris; dangerous coastal conditions.
impacts.transport: Bridge closures, rail speed restrictions, ferry and flight cancellations.
impacts.coast: Wave overtopping; flooding if the storm coincides with high tide.

Track errors of 100 km can change the worst-affected region.

deep-atlantic-low.frequency: Seasonally common from October to March; plausible in spring; uncommon in summer.

climate.observed: There is no clear long-term trend in UK storminess in the observational record, which shows large decadal variability.
climate.projected: Projections suggest a possible small increase in winter wind storms over the UK, but with low confidence; rainfall in storms is expected to increase with warming.

safety: Avoid coastal paths and seafronts in storms; large waves can sweep people away.
Check travel before setting out and expect disruption.

events.title: Burns' Day Storm
events.summary: An intense depression tracked across southern Scotland in daylight, bringing severe gales and storm-force winds to much of England and Wales. Winds affected a much larger area than in October 1987 and struck during the day, so there were more casualties: 47 lives were lost.
observations: Wind speeds comparable to October 1987, and higher over parts of southern England and Wales.
47 deaths.

events.title: Carlisle floods
events.summary: Prolonged rain over the Lake District and Pennines drained into the River Eden. Three people were killed; it was the worst flood in Carlisle since 1822.
observations: A near-stationary front in a westerly airstream, followed by a very deep depression.

events.title: Strong winds 10–12 March 2008
events.summary: A deep low crossed southern Ireland, Wales and Lincolnshire. Strong winds, low pressure and a high tide combined to bring coastal flooding to parts of the south coast.
observations: 946 hPa west of Ireland at 00 UTC on 10 March.

events.title: Cornwall floods
events.summary: A line of intense rain developed with a deep autumn low, flooding St Blazey, St Austell, Mevagissey and Lostwithiel. More than 100 properties flooded and the main line to Penzance closed.
observations: 40 mm or more in two hours in places.

events.title: Winter storm, 3 January 2012
events.summary: The Central Belt's most severe storm for 13 years (since 26 December 1998), part of a turbulent spell from late November.
observations: Gusts well over 70 knots (81 mph) in southern Scotland.

events.title: Storms Ali and Bronagh
events.summary: A powerful jet stream drove two storms that marked an emphatic transition from the fine summer of 2018 to autumn. Ali was one of the most notable storms at that time of year in recent decades.
observations: Ali: gusts widely over 60 knots (69 mph) across the north.
Bronagh: well over 50 mm of rain on upland Wales and the south Pennines.

events.title: Storm Hannah
events.summary: For Wales, one of the most significant April storms in 50 years. Trees coming into leaf were brought down.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) in exposed west Wales.

events.title: Strong winds, 2 November 2019
events.summary: A low brought very strong winds to south Wales and the English south coast. A woman was killed by a falling tree in Dorset.
observations: 95 knots (109 mph) at Needles Old Battery; 72 knots at Plymouth; 71 knots at Culdrose.

events.title: Storm Ciara
events.summary: The most significant storm for gust speeds across England and Wales overall since 12 February 2014, with persistent heavy rain over the uplands of north-west England. The Humber Bridge closed for only the second time in its history.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots widely across England and Wales.
Over a month's rain in about 18 hours in parts of West Yorkshire.

events.title: Storms Ellen and Francis
events.summary: A strong jet stream drove deep lows across the UK in late August: two of the most notable August storms of the last 50 years. Trees in full leaf on saturated ground came down; beach huts at Woolacombe were washed away.
observations: 69 knots (79 mph) at Capel Curig (Ellen); 70 knots (81 mph) at Needles Old Battery (Francis).

events.title: Storm Agnes
events.summary: An intense low enhanced by energy from Tropical Storm Ophelia, weakening before it reached the UK. Impacts were relatively modest overall.
observations: 73 knots (84 mph) at Capel Curig — the equal-highest September gust for Wales.

events.title: Storm Ciarán
events.summary: An exceptionally severe storm for the time of year. Its track meant northern France and the Channel Islands bore the brunt, with winds comparable to south-east England in October 1987; for the UK, recorded winds were fairly typical of a major Atlantic storm. Intense squally rain bands crossed the Channel Islands with very large hail and a reported tornado in Jersey.
observations: 953.6 hPa at Culdrose and St Catherine's Point, which the Met Office reports as England's lowest November pressure.
Gusts of 60 to 70 knots (69 to 81 mph) on the south coast.

events.title: Storm Kathleen
events.summary: An unusually deep low for the time of year. Kathleen and storm Noa (April 2023) were the most significant April windstorms since April 2013.
observations: Gusts widely over 50 knots on western and northern coasts.

events.title: Storm Amy
events.summary: An unusually severe, though not unprecedented, October storm for Scotland and Northern Ireland, with heavy rain on top of the wind.
observations: Gusts over 80 knots (92 mph) at the most exposed sites.
100 to 150 mm of rain on western and northern uplands in the first four days of October.

events.title: Storm Dave
events.summary: The most severe April windstorm since storm naming began in autumn 2015, judged by the number of stations exceeding 50 and 60 knots. The most severe April windstorm in the observational record remains 1 April 1994.
observations: Gust of 81 knots (93 mph) at Capel Curig — its highest April gust in a 30-year record.
UK April gust record: 87 knots (100 mph) at Flat Holm, 1 April 1994.

cyclone-family.name: A succession of low-pressure systems
cyclone-family.summary: Several lows cross the UK in quick succession, each arriving before the land and rivers have recovered from the last. The cumulative impact can far exceed that of any single storm.
body: Taken individually, the first storms of the 2013–14 winter were notable but not exceptional; together, at least 12 major storms from mid-December to mid-February made it the stormiest period the UK had experienced for at least 20 years. The Met Office made the same point about late November 2012: individually unexceptional rain events whose rapid succession on saturated ground caused widespread flooding.
Successive storms also hamper recovery: Storm Barra (December 2021) delayed reconnection of homes still without power after Storm Arwen.
regions: Whichever region lies under the storm track receives repeated impacts.
Rain accumulates on western hills with each system.

essential: A persistent, active storm track over the UK.
Lows forming in sequence along the jet.

outcomes: Repeated gales and heavy rain every 1–3 days.
Escalating river flooding and groundwater rise.
Coastal damage accumulating over successive high tides.

impacts.rivers: Flooding builds as catchments never drain.

signals: Medium-range ensembles
A persistent cyclonic regime is often well signalled a week or more ahead.
Individual storm details are not.
Soil moisture and river levels
Show how primed catchments are for the next rain.
Local flood response varies.
cyclone-family.frequency: Seasonally common in autumn and winter.

events.title: The wet autumn of 2000
events.summary: The wettest autumn on record for England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the UK (series from 1914). Rivers rose to record levels; 10,000 homes and businesses flooded at 700 locations — the most extensive flooding since the snowmelt floods of March 1947.
observations: Highest autumn value in the England and Wales rainfall series from 1766.

events.title: January 2005 stormy spells
events.summary: Two stormy spells in the first half of the month. Northern England took a battering on the 7th and 8th: lorries overturned and 80,000 customers lost power in north-east England.
observations: Many wind-speed records were set during the month.

events.title: Early winter storms, late 2011
events.summary: A powerful jet stream sent a succession of deep depressions across the north. The 8 December storm was the most significant for Scotland since January 2005.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots widely in Scotland; mountain summits well over 100 knots (115 mph).

events.title: Winter storms, December 2013 to February 2014
events.summary: A succession of at least 12 major winter storms from mid-December to mid-February: the stormiest period the UK had experienced for at least 20 years. The 5 December storm drove a major North Sea surge. As rain accumulated, concern shifted from wind to flooding — the Somerset Levels were under water for much of the winter and the Thames flooded through Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Surrey. On 5 February the railway at Dawlish was left suspended when its foundations were washed away.
observations: 5 December 2013 surge: 2 m above predicted high water, coinciding with high tide.
Around 6 major storms from late January to mid-February, 2 to 3 days apart.

events.title: Wettest calendar month on record, December 2015
events.summary: A persistent, exceptionally mild south-westerly flow of tropical maritime air brought a series of Atlantic lows, including storms Eva and Frank. Boxing Day rain flooded parts of Lancashire, north Manchester and West Yorkshire.
observations: December 2015 was the wettest calendar month for the UK in a series from 1910.
Also easily the mildest December in the UK series from 1910 and the Central England Temperature series from 1659.

events.title: Storm Dennis
events.summary: A week after Ciara, Dennis brought 50 to 100 mm or more to western uplands on saturated ground. A red warning for rain covered parts of south Wales; the Wye and Severn were reported at their highest-ever levels and over 1,400 homes and businesses flooded.
observations: Over 600 flood warnings and alerts from the Environment Agency.

events.title: Storms Malik and Corrie
events.summary: Two storms 36 hours apart brought damaging north-westerly winds. Two people were killed by falling trees.
observations: Corrie: 80 knots (92 mph) at Stornoway Airport; 79 knots at Inverbervie.

events.title: Storms Dudley, Eunice and Franklin
events.summary: Three named storms in a week, the first time since naming began in 2015/16. Eunice brought two rare red warnings and was the most severe and damaging storm to affect England and Wales since February 2014. Four people died in the UK and Ireland from falling trees and over a million homes lost power.
observations: Gust of 106 knots (122 mph) at Needles Old Battery, Isle of Wight — a new England gust record.
Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) widely across southern England.
Severe coastal flooding in the Severn Estuary avoided: the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in places.

events.title: Storms Isha and Jocelyn
events.summary: Two storms in quick succession driven by a powerful jet stream, itself intensified by a large temperature contrast across North America. Isha brought an amber warning over more than half the UK and an overnight red warning for north-east Scotland.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) in Northumberland.
Most significant widespread wind storm since Eunice in February 2022.

events.title: Storm Chandra
events.summary: Part of a sequence of lows in late January: the whole-month January average fell widely across south-west England, north-east Scotland and eastern Northern Ireland in eight days. Widespread flooding in Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
observations: Over 50 mm widely and up to 100 mm on high ground in the worst-affected areas.

persistent-anticyclone.name: Persistent anticyclonic conditions
persistent-anticyclone.summary: High pressure settles over or close to the UK for an extended spell: light winds, little rain, and weather decided by the season and by how much cloud is trapped beneath the high.
body: Air sinks and warms in an anticyclone, creating a temperature inversion that acts as a lid. With little cloud, days are sunny and nights cold — frost and fog in winter, heat in summer. With moisture trapped under the inversion, it can instead stay grey and dull for days (anticyclonic gloom).

Persistent high pressure was behind the UK's warmest, sunniest spring (2025) and the hot, dry summer of 2018, and in winter behind the Great Smog of 1952, when an inversion trapped coal smoke over London.
regions: Can cover the whole country; edges may be cloudier or catch weak fronts.
Largest temperature swings and most fog and frost.

essential: A slow-moving high over or near the UK.
favourable: Dry air mass (sunshine) or moist air trapped below an inversion (gloom).

outcomes: Little or no rain for days or weeks.
Summer: sunshine, warmth, heat; possible drought.
Winter: frost, fog, freezing fog — or persistent grey stratus.
Poor air quality under strong inversions.

impacts.agriculture: Drought stress in summer; frost in spring.
impacts.people: Heat or cold health risks; air-quality episodes.

signals: Pressure charts
A high centred over the UK with weak gradients.
Cloud cover under highs is notoriously hard to forecast.
Upper-air soundings
Show the inversion height and moisture trapped below it.
Small moisture differences decide sun versus gloom.
persistent-anticyclone.frequency: Seasonally common from spring to early autumn; plausible in winter.

persistent-low.name: Unusually persistent low pressure
persistent-low.summary: A low or trough becomes slow-moving over or near the UK, giving day after day of showers or longer rain, often with thunder in the warmer months.
body: Where a low stalls rather than racing through, the same areas can receive repeated heavy showers or bands of rain. In May 2024 a slow-moving front around a low off the east coast gave northern England its wettest spring day in a series from 1891.
In summer, persistent low pressure means cool, cloudy, showery weather and can bring flooding where heavy showers repeat over the same places.

essential: A slow-moving or cut-off low near the UK.
favourable: Blocking downstream that prevents the low from moving east.

persistent-low.duration: Several days to a few weeks.

slow-trough.name: Slow-moving upper trough
slow-trough.summary: A slow-moving trough of cold air in the upper atmosphere sits over the UK. Cold air aloft over sun-warmed ground makes the atmosphere unstable, so heavy, often thundery showers with hail develop day after day.
body: The Met Office explains that thunderstorms develop when warm air lies underneath much colder air. A trough of cold air aloft provides that contrast even when surface temperatures are only modest, which is why spring is such a showery season: the sun is strong but the air above is still wintry.

In summer a slow trough approaching a hot, humid air mass is one of the classic triggers of thunderstorm outbreaks; the Met Office describes Spanish plume storms as forming when cooler air at height advances from the west.
regions: Showers form widely; heaviest inland where heating is greatest.

essential: Cold air in the mid and upper troposphere.
favourable: Slow movement, so showers repeat in the same areas.

outcomes: Sunshine and heavy showers, with hail and thunder.

impacts.transport: Sudden hail and spray on roads.
impacts.agriculture: Hail damage to crops is possible.

cut-off-low.name: Cut-off low
cut-off-low.summary: A low becomes detached from the main jet stream and drifts slowly and unpredictably — sometimes westward. It can bring days of rain and thunderstorms, often from unusual directions.
body: When the jet buckles strongly, part of a trough can be cut off south of the main flow. With nothing to steer it, the low wanders slowly; rain bands can rotate around it for days, and its unusual position can bring easterly or south-easterly flows of moist, unstable air.

In late September 2024 a series of lows in a south-easterly flow of unstable air produced thunderstorms and torrential rain, making it the wettest calendar month on record for Oxfordshire and Bedfordshire in a series from 1836.

Easterly flows around lows to the south can bring prolonged rain to eastern coasts.

favourable: Warm, moist air drawn around the low.

outcomes: Prolonged, slow-moving rain, sometimes from the east.

impacts.transport: Road closures from flooding.

events.title: Exceptionally wet weather, May 2024
events.summary: A slow-moving front around a low off the east coast. A schoolgirl died in a mudslide in North Yorkshire and the West Coast Main Line closed.
observations: 22 May: northern England's wettest spring day in a series from 1891.
75 to 100 mm in the wettest places.

events.title: Wettest month on record for parts of the Midlands
events.summary: A series of lows in a south-easterly flow of unstable air brought thunderstorms and torrential rain; several hundred properties flooded across Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire and Oxfordshire.
observations: Oxfordshire and Bedfordshire recorded their wettest calendar month on record (series from 1836).
Oxford recorded its wettest calendar month for 250 years.

developing-cyclone.name: Developing and deepening extratropical cyclone
developing-cyclone.summary: A low forms as a wave on a front beneath the jet stream and deepens as warm air rises and cold air sinks around it — the life cycle behind most UK wind and rain.
body: The Met Office explains that fronts separate warm and cold air, and their interaction creates and develops wet and windy weather. Conveyor belts of warm air (rising) and cold air (sinking) wrap around the low and feed it. A wave on a trailing cold front can develop into a new "secondary" low, sometimes rapidly.
Most developing lows are routine; a minority deepen explosively. The difference often comes down to the strength of support from the jet stream and the amount of warm, moist air available.
regions: Developing lows can cross any part of the UK.

essential: A temperature contrast along a front.
Upper-level support from the jet stream.
favourable: Warm, moist air in the warm sector (energy from condensation).

outcomes: Bands of rain from warm and cold fronts.
Strengthening winds as the low deepens.
developing-cyclone.duration: Lows typically develop over one to two days.
signals: Satellite imagery

explosive-cyclogenesis.name: Rapid cyclogenesis ("weather bomb")

monthNotes.oct: The Great Storm of 1987 deepened rapidly over the Bay of Biscay before crossing southern England.
monthNotes.nov: Storm Ciarán (2023) set England's lowest November pressure on record.

explosive-cyclogenesis.summary: A low whose central pressure falls at least 24 millibars in 24 hours. Violent winds can develop around it within a few hours.
body: The Met Office describes a weather bomb as an unofficial term for a low whose central pressure falls 24 mb in 24 hours, a process called explosive cyclogenesis. Rapid acceleration of air in the jet stream removes air from the column, lowering surface pressure; air converging in from the surroundings spins faster and faster, like an ice skater drawing in their arms.

Explosively deepening lows are where sting jets can form — the narrow cores of extreme winds behind the Great Storm of 1987. They are also harder to forecast precisely, because small errors in timing or position grow quickly.
regions: Most explosively deepening lows pass closest to the north and west.
Rare but very damaging when the track is further south (1987, 2022).

favourable: Low developing in the left exit region of a jet streak.

outcomes: Damaging, possibly extreme gusts in a short window.
explosive-cyclogenesis.duration: The most intense winds often last only a few hours.

impacts.people: Danger to life from falling trees and debris.

signals: Pressure falls in models and observations
Forecast deepening of 24 hPa or more in 24 hours.
Exact depth and track are uncertain until close to the event.
Satellite cloud-head and dry-intrusion features
Indicate rapid development and sting-jet potential.

events.title: The Great Storm of 1987
events.summary: A depression that formed over the Bay of Biscay deepened rapidly and crossed southern England overnight. 18 people were killed in England and about 15 million trees were blown down. Forecast models in the final day suggested the worst would stay over the Channel.
observations: Strongest UK gust 100 knots at Shoreham (Sussex).

Analysis suggested such conditions over land in south and south-east England might be expected on average once in 200 years; over the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland, once every 30 to 40 years.

events.title: Autumn storm, 28 October 2013

events.title: Storm Ciarán

Its track meant northern France and the Channel Islands bore the brunt, with winds comparable to south-east England in October 1987; for the UK, recorded winds were fairly typical of a major Atlantic storm. Intense squally rain bands crossed the Channel Islands with very large hail and a reported tornado in Jersey.

settled-to-unsettled.summary: A settled spell ends as high pressure gives way to Atlantic lows or a thundery trough. After a long dry spell the first heavy rain can run off baked ground rather than soaking in.

An Atlantic breakdown brings wind and frontal rain, often marking the switch from summer to autumn — as with Storm Alex in October 2020, after which the UK recorded its wettest day on record.
Dry, hard ground can increase run-off from the first heavy downpours, so surface-water flooding can happen even though rivers and groundwater are low.

sudden-stratospheric-warming.name: Sudden stratospheric warming (SSW)

monthNotes.jan: SSW effects have been connected to the cold spells of 2009–10 and 2013 and the 2018 "Beast from the East" (Met Office).

sudden-stratospheric-warming.summary: The winter polar vortex high in the stratosphere weakens or reverses, and the stratosphere over the Arctic warms by up to about 50 °C in days. Weeks later it can — but does not always — tilt the odds towards blocking and cold easterlies over the UK.
body: The Met Office explains that strong westerly winds normally circle the pole in the stratosphere in winter. In some years they weaken or reverse; air descends and compresses over the polar cap, warming rapidly. The effects can work down to the troposphere over the following weeks, making the jet stream "snake" more and favouring blocking highs over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia.

The Met Office is careful to say SSWs do not happen every year and do not always affect UK weather when they do. Individual SSWs can be predicted about a week ahead, and their surface influence usually takes a few weeks to arrive — which makes them useful for monthly outlooks but not a guarantee of snow.

essential: Breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex.
favourable: Downward propagation of the easterly anomaly to the troposphere.

polar-maritime.name: Polar maritime air (Pm)

polar-maritime.summary: Air from near Greenland and northern Canada that has crossed a long stretch of relatively warm ocean. It arrives cool and unstable: bright, blustery weather with showers.
body: Polar maritime air is the UK's most common air mass. It starts cold and dry but is warmed and moistened from below on its long journey over the North Atlantic, which makes it unstable. Cumulus and cumulonimbus clouds build, giving showers that are most frequent on western and northern coasts and hills, and visibility is usually excellent between them.

In winter the sea is warmer than the land, so showers are most frequent near western coasts and by night, and can fall as hail, sleet or snow on hills. In spring and summer the land heats strongly by day, so showers build inland in the afternoon and die away in the evening.

body: Arctic maritime air has had little time over warm water, so it arrives very cold — the Met Office notes northerly winds bring air straight from the Arctic over a cold sea. Its sea track does add enough heat and moisture for heavy snow showers on north-facing coasts and hills, especially northern Scotland and, in a north-easterly, eastern coasts.

Inland and in the south, away from the showers, it often means sunshine, a biting wind and severe frosts on clear nights. Showers can be carried far inland along lines (for example through the Cheshire Gap from the Irish Sea).

polar-continental.summary: Air from the frozen interior of northern Europe and Russia, reaching the UK on an easterly wind. In winter it is the coldest air mass the UK gets; crossing the North Sea it gains moisture for snow showers on eastern coasts.
body: In winter the continental interior becomes intensely cold. When high pressure lies to the north or north-east, an easterly wind brings this air west. Over land it stays dry, so much of the UK gets crisp sunshine; the short North Sea crossing, however, warms and moistens the lowest layers and can produce bands of heavy snow showers that drive into eastern Scotland and England.
Air of this type was behind the severe spells of early 1947, late February 2018 and February 2021, when daytime temperatures stayed below freezing and a strong east wind added severe wind chill.

monthNotes.dec: December 2015, easily the UK's mildest December on record, was dominated by tropical maritime air.

tropical-maritime.summary: Warm, moist air from the subtropical Atlantic near the Azores, arriving on a south-westerly wind. Mild, humid and cloudy: low cloud, drizzle and hill fog, with very mild nights in winter.
body: Tropical maritime air is cooled from below as it travels north over progressively cooler water, which makes it stable at low levels. The result is extensive low cloud, drizzle and fog on coasts and hills, especially in the west. In winter it gives exceptionally mild nights; the Met Office notes overcast nights kept minimum temperatures above 10 °C widely over New Year 2021/22.

Tropical maritime air also carries large amounts of water vapour. Lifted over mountains or along a slow-moving front, it can produce prolonged, very heavy rain — the warm-conveyor and atmospheric-river events behind several of the UK's rainfall records.

tropical-continental.summary: Hot, dry air from North Africa and Iberia, drawn north over France on a southerly wind. The source of the UK's highest temperatures.
body: Tropical continental air reaches the UK when high pressure lies to the east and low pressure to the west, setting up a southerly flow. The air has crossed hot land rather than sea, so it is hot and often hazy. The 40.3 °C UK record (19 July 2022) and the 38.7 °C record before it (25 July 2019) were both set as hot air moved north from the near continent.

The same air, lifted over cooler air or undercut by an Atlantic trough, can become the warm layer at the heart of a "Spanish plume", which acts as a lid on convection until it breaks and thunderstorms erupt.

returning-polar-maritime.summary: Polar maritime air that has travelled south over the Atlantic and then curved back towards the UK from the south-west. Warmer and more stable at low levels than direct Pm air, but still cold aloft.
body: On its loop south the air is warmed and moistened from below, then cooled slightly again on the way back north. It arrives from the south-west — the same direction as tropical air — but is noticeably cooler. Cloud is often layered and broken, with showers or patchy rain; skies can clear well inland, with fog or frost on calm nights.

returning-tropical-maritime.name: Tropical maritime air on a curved (returning) track
returning-tropical-maritime.summary: Tropical maritime air that reaches the UK on a looping path around a low — for example from the south or south-east rather than the usual south-west. It is not a standard named class in the UK system, so it is described here by its behaviour.
body: Note on terminology: the traditional UK classification recognises "returning polar maritime" air but not a formally defined "returning tropical maritime" class. In practice, warm, moist subtropical air can be drawn around a low and arrive from an unusual direction — south or even east — after part of its track over land or the near continent. That changes its character: drier and warmer by day if it has crossed France in summer, cloudier and damper if it has spent longer over the sea.
Such air commonly feeds the warm, moist side of slow-moving fronts and cut-off lows, which is why it appears in several of the UK's heavy rainfall events in eastern areas.

modified-continental.name: Modified continental air
aka: continental air over the North Sea
modified-continental.summary: Continental air whose lowest layers have been altered by the North Sea. In winter the sea warms it and feeds snow showers; in spring and summer the sea cools it and produces low cloud and haar on eastern coasts while the west is warm and sunny.
body: The North Sea's effect on easterly air changes sign with the seasons. In winter the sea is warmer than the air, so the air becomes unstable and showery. In spring and early summer the sea is colder than the air, so the lowest layers are cooled to saturation: the Met Office notes coastal fog (haar) is frequent on the east coast in spring and summer when warm air moves over the cool North Sea.
This is why an easterly spring day can bring 20 °C and sunshine in Glasgow, Cardiff or Belfast while Aberdeen, Edinburgh and Newcastle sit at 10 °C under fog.

northerly-airflow.name: Northerly airflow

northerly-airflow.summary: Wind from the north brings the coldest air for the season, with showers on north-facing coasts and dry, sunny but chilly weather to the south.
body: A northerly usually develops between high pressure over the Atlantic and low pressure over Scandinavia. Its character depends on the source of the air (Arctic or polar maritime) and the season. Northern Scotland, the northern isles and north-facing coasts take the showers; areas to the south, sheltered by hills, are often dry with frost at night.

Unusual wind direction can matter for damage. The Met Office suggested the northerly direction of Storm Arwen's strongest winds may have been an additional factor in the number of trees brought down, since trees are adapted to the prevailing westerlies.

body: Easterlies blow when high pressure lies to the north or north-east of the UK. Their character depends on the season and the temperature of the continent. In winter they can bring severe cold and North Sea snow showers. In spring the continent is still cool and the air dry, so easterlies give the classic "dry easterly" spell: lots of sunshine in the west, cool and cloudy on eastern coasts, and drying soils. In summer an easterly can carry continental heat.

widespread-snowfall.name: Widespread snowfall

monthNotes.jan: January and February are more likely than December: the Met Office gives an average of 3.3 days of lying snow in January and 3.4 in February versus 3.0 in December (1991–2020).
monthNotes.mar: Possible early in the month in cold years (2013, 2018).

widespread-snowfall.summary: Snow falls across a large part of the UK, including low ground, and settles. It needs cold air in place AND a source of moisture — and in a maritime climate those rarely coincide.
body: The Met Office explains that UK snow needs cold enough air (usually from the north or east, or a long cold anticyclonic spell) and a supply of moisture. The most common UK wind is south-westerly, bringing mild Atlantic air and rain; cold easterlies, by contrast, are often too dry. Widespread snow therefore tends to come when cold air already over the UK meets a weather front from the south or west, or when a strong cold flow picks up moisture over the North Sea or Irish Sea.

Precipitation can fall as snow at air temperatures up to about 2 °C, and the heaviest UK snowfalls tend to occur between 0 and 2 °C. That is why the boundary between rain and snow can be a matter of a fraction of a degree, a few hundred metres of altitude or a few miles.

frontal-snow.name: Frontal snow
frontal-snow.summary: A weather front pushes into cold air already over the UK. Mild air rides up over the cold, and the precipitation falls through the cold layer as snow — often heavy, but with a sharp, hard-to-forecast edge.
body: The Met Office describes this as the most difficult situation for snow forecasting: when warm air meets cold air, the warm air slides up over the cold; precipitation falls into the colder air below, but in time the air mixes, the cold layer warms and rain becomes more likely. There is often a fine line between who sees snow and who sees rain.

Storm Emma (1 March 2018) is a classic example: mild, moist air pushed north into very cold air, giving heavy snow across southern and south-west England and south Wales and a second red warning. Storm Goretti (January 2026) brought widespread lying snow on its northern flank across much of Wales, the West Midlands and the South Pennines.

convective-snow-showers.name: Convective snow showers
convective-snow-showers.summary: Very cold air crossing relatively warm sea becomes unstable and builds showers that fall as snow. Some places stay dry and sunny; others under persistent shower bands can get large accumulations.
body: The Met Office explains that cold air can pick up enough moisture on its short journey across the North Sea to form showers, and that hills and mountains enhance precipitation as the air rises. Showers often organise into bands or "streamers" aligned with the wind and can repeat over the same places for hours.

Northern and north-east Scotland had 30 to 50 cm of lying snow in early January 2026 from persistent northerly snow showers — depths the Met Office described as comparatively unusual, particularly in a warming climate.

north-sea-snow-showers.summary: In a cold easterly or north-easterly, the North Sea warms and moistens the lowest air, building bands of heavy snow showers that drive into eastern Scotland and England.

In late February 2018 showers organised along convergence lines; persistent heavy snow along one through Scotland's Central Belt led to a red warning on 28 February.

irish-sea-snow-showers.name: Irish Sea snow showers
irish-sea-snow-showers.summary: In a cold northerly or north-westerly, showers form over the Irish Sea and can be carried inland along a narrow line — through the Cheshire Gap into the Midlands, or onto Pembrokeshire, Anglesey, the Isle of Man and Northern Ireland.
body: The Irish Sea acts like a smaller North Sea: cold air crossing it is warmed and moistened, and showers form. With a steady wind direction, the showers can line up into a streamer that delivers snow repeatedly to the same narrow corridor far inland, while places a few miles either side stay dry.
Forecasters' informal names for some of these streamers (such as the "Cheshire Gap streamer") reflect how often the geography channels them, but each event depends on precise wind direction.

upland-snow.summary: Precipitation falls as snow above a certain height (the freezing level) and as rain below. The UK's high ground — especially the Scottish Highlands — sees snow far more often than lowland areas.
body: The Met Office explains that hilltops are often snow-covered when there is none at ground level because the freezing level — where the air is at 0 °C — can lie anywhere from about 200 ft upwards. Air rising over hills cools, so they also squeeze out more precipitation.
The snowiest UK stations are high-altitude sites in the Cairngorms and eastern Highlands: Cairngorm Chairlift averages 75.2 days a year with snow lying at 0900, and Braemar 47.6 (1991–2020).

easterly-snow-event.name: Easterly snow event ("Beast from the East")

monthNotes.feb: The most famous recent example began on 26 February 2018.
monthNotes.mar: Late March 2013 saw prolonged easterly cold and heavy snow on 22–24 March.

easterly-snow-event.summary: A Scandinavian or Siberian high drives bitterly cold continental air west across the UK. Snow showers pile up in the east; if an Atlantic system then pushes into the cold air, a major snowstorm can follow.
body: "Beast from the East" is a media nickname, used by the Met Office for the late February–early March 2018 event. Daytime temperatures stayed widely below freezing with a strong east wind and significant accumulations of snow across much of the country, and two red warnings were issued: one for persistent heavy snow along a convergence line through Scotland's Central Belt, the second when Storm Emma pushed mild, moist air into the cold air over the south-west. Freezing rain followed.
The Met Office links several such events (2009–10, 2013 and 2018) to sudden stratospheric warmings, while stressing that a warming does not always affect UK weather.

Severe if an Atlantic low runs into the cold (Storm Emma 2018).

northerly-snow-event.name: Northerly snow event
northerly-snow-event.summary: An Arctic northerly brings frequent snow showers to northern Scotland and north-facing coasts, and occasionally a small, intense low or trough that carries snow further south.
body: Northern and north-east Scotland, Orkney and Shetland are most exposed. In early January 2026 a northerly flow brought persistent snow showers and 30 to 50 cm of lying snow in the worst affected areas, prompting a major incident declaration in Aberdeenshire.
Further south, northerlies usually bring dry, sunny, cold weather — unless a trough or "polar low" forms in the flow and runs south, bringing a band of snow more widely.

coastal-snow-showers.name: Snow showers in coastal areas
coastal-snow-showers.summary: In cold onshore winds, showers form over the sea and deposit snow, sleet and hail on exposed coasts — often more there than a few miles inland, where showers fade.
body: Because the sea feeds the showers, coasts facing the wind get most of them; snow may fail to settle right at the shoreline if the sea air is marginally too warm, yet build up on rising ground just inland. Which coasts are affected depends entirely on wind direction: north-facing coasts in northerlies, east coasts in easterlies, west coasts in north-westerlies.

essential: Cold onshore wind over relatively warm sea.

outcomes: Wintry showers on coasts and adjacent hills.

blizzard-drifting.name: Blizzards and drifting snow
blizzard-drifting.summary: Falling or lying snow driven by strong wind. The Met Office defines a blizzard as moderate or heavy snow with winds of 30 mph or more and visibility of 200 m or less.
body: The Met Office definition requires moderate or heavy falling snow (continuous or frequent showers), wind speeds of 30 mph or more and fairly extensive snow cover reducing visibility to 200 m or less. A "ground blizzard" can occur even after the snow has stopped, as strong wind lifts lying snow. Drifting needs dry, powdery snow (temperature and dew point below 0 °C) and winds of at least 10 mph.
Drifts can be extraordinary: up to seven metres deep in Scotland in March 1947, and up to six metres in Wales and south-west England in the blizzard of 29–30 December 1962.

freezing-rain.name: Freezing rain
freezing-rain.summary: Rain falls through a shallow layer of sub-zero air at the surface, becomes supercooled and freezes on contact, coating everything in clear ice. Rare in the UK, but dangerous when it happens.
body: The Met Office describes the profile needed: snow high in the cloud melts as it falls through a layer above freezing (a "warm nose"), then falls into sub-zero air just above the ground, where the droplets become supercooled and freeze on impact. It typically occurs at the end of a cold period when milder air rises over the cold air at the surface.

In January 1996, after cold easterlies, a low moving north across southern England brought freezing rain to Wales, south-west England and the Midlands; the Birmingham area reported a 50% increase in hospital admissions and power was disrupted in South Wales. Freezing rain also followed the 2018 "Beast from the East" and caused multiple accidents during Storm Deirdre (December 2018).

body: Freezing drizzle can form without a warm layer: in shallow, moist stratus cloud that never gets cold enough at the top to produce ice crystals, droplets stay liquid below 0 °C. It most often occurs under cold anticyclones or in light easterlies with low cloud, and can glaze roads and pavements without anything dramatic seeming to happen.

sleet-transition.name: Sleet and rain–snow transitions
sleet-transition.summary: Precipitation falling as a mixture of rain and snow, or changing between them, as temperatures hover close to the melting point.
body: The Met Office notes sleet has no internationally agreed definition but is reported in UK observations as a mix of rain and snow: snow that has partly melted on the way down. It also describes ice pellets (snowflakes that melt and then refreeze while falling) and snow grains (the solid equivalent of drizzle).

Rain can turn to snow when heavy precipitation drags the freezing level down by melting and evaporative cooling, and snow can turn to rain as milder air mixes in. These transitions are what make UK snow forecasts so finely balanced.

severe-air-frost.name: Severe air frost
severe-air-frost.summary: Air temperatures fall well below freezing — around −10 °C or lower — usually on clear, calm nights over snow cover, especially in sheltered valleys and glens.
body: Severe frosts need very cold air, clear skies, light winds and ideally snow cover, which radiates heat away efficiently and insulates the ground. Cold air drains into valleys and hollows, so the lowest temperatures are found in places like Braemar and Altnaharra in Scotland or Shropshire in the 1982 cold spell. The UK record minimum is −27.2 °C, reached at Braemar (1895 and 1982) and Altnaharra (1995).
In February 2021 Braemar fell to −23.0 °C, the UK's lowest temperature since December 1995. In December 2022, minimums fell widely to −5 to −10 °C even in cities and on coasts.

outcomes: Freezing of lakes and rivers in prolonged spells.

freezing-fog.summary: Fog at sub-zero temperatures. Its droplets stay liquid (supercooled) but freeze on contact with surfaces, forming feathery rime and icing roads.
body: The Met Office explains freezing fog forms like normal fog but below 0 °C: the droplets become supercooled because liquid water needs a surface to freeze upon. Where they touch something they freeze, forming rime on the windward side of objects. In the UK it typically happens in winter with temperatures around freezing, clear skies and calm conditions; rime at low levels is fairly rare but more frequent on hills.

Rime forms on hilltops in freezing hill fog.

favourable: Winter anticyclone, light winds, moist ground.

impacts.transport: Combined fog and ice on roads; aviation delays.

Fog forming with temperatures below zero.

safety: Drive slowly with dipped headlights in fog.

anticyclonic-gloom.name: Persistent low cloud and anticyclonic gloom
aka: persistent cloud and low temperatures under winter high pressure
anticyclonic-gloom.summary: High pressure traps a layer of moist air under its inversion. Instead of crisp sunshine, the UK sits under a lid of grey stratus or stratocumulus for days — dry, dull and chilly.
body: Under an anticyclone, sinking, warming air forms an inversion that acts as a lid. If moisture is trapped beneath it — often after the high has drawn in air over the sea — a sheet of low cloud forms and the weak winter sun cannot break it up. Days are grey, nights relatively mild because the cloud prevents frost. The Met Office case study of February 1947 notes sunshine in the Midlands and south was only about 40% of average, with no sun at Kew, Nottingham and Edgbaston on 22 of 28 days.
regions: Gloom is most persistent inland where the cloud is trapped.
Onshore flow off the North Sea feeds the cloud.
Some western areas may break into sunshine.

essential: A slow-moving anticyclone with a strong inversion.

outcomes: Days of grey, dry weather with little temperature range.
Poor air quality under the inversion.
signals: Soundings showing a moist layer capped by an inversion
Indicate trapped cloud.
Models often struggle to clear or hold such cloud correctly.
anticyclonic-gloom.frequency: Common in late autumn and winter anticyclones.

mild-winter-spell.name: Exceptionally mild winter weather

monthNotes.feb: The UK winter record of 21.2 °C was set at Kew Gardens on 26 February 2019.
monthNotes.jan: UK January record: 19.9 °C at Achfary on 28 January 2024, a föhn effect.
monthNotes.dec: UK December record: 18.7 °C at Achfary on 28 December 2019, also föhn.

mild-winter-spell.summary: Temperatures far above normal for winter, from either a strong tropical maritime south-westerly or a warm southerly from Iberia and North Africa — sometimes boosted locally by föhn.
body: Two routes lead to winter warmth. A persistent south-westerly of tropical maritime air gives mild, cloudy, often wet weather with exceptionally high minimum temperatures — December 2015 was easily the UK's mildest on record. A southerly flow around a continental high gives sunnier, drier warmth, as in February 2019.

The highest winter temperatures are often not in the south but in north-west Scotland or north Wales, where föhn warms air descending lee slopes. The Met Office notes föhn is the primary cause of highly localised winter temperature extremes in Scotland and Wales.
regions: Föhn on the lee side of Snowdonia (north Wales coast).

essential: A mild south-westerly or southerly flow.
favourable: Föhn on the lee side of mountains.

outcomes: Daytime highs in the mid to upper teens.
Spring flowers and growth unseasonably early.

impacts.agriculture: Early growth vulnerable to later frost.
impacts.rivers: If wet, flood risk from heavy rain.

signals: 850 hPa temperatures and air-mass source
Very warm air for the season.
Föhn maxima are hard to forecast exactly.
mild-winter-spell.frequency: Mild spells are common in UK winters; record-breaking warmth is uncommon to rare.

climate.projected: Winters are projected to become milder on average.
