events.title: January warmth at Aboyne
events.summary: Record-equalling January warmth in Aberdeenshire.
observations: 18.3 °C at Aboyne, equalling the then UK January record (Aber, 1958 and 1971).

events.title: Wettest calendar month on record, December 2015
events.summary: A persistent, exceptionally mild south-westerly flow of tropical maritime air brought a series of Atlantic lows, including storms Eva and Frank. Boxing Day rain flooded parts of Lancashire, north Manchester and West Yorkshire.
observations: December 2015 was the wettest calendar month for the UK in a series from 1910.
Also easily the mildest December in the UK series from 1910 and the Central England Temperature series from 1659.

events.title: Winter warmth, February 2019
events.summary: High pressure over the near continent drew an exceptionally mild southerly flow from Iberia and North Africa.
observations: 21.2 °C at Kew Gardens on 26 February — the UK's highest temperature on record for a winter month.

events.title: Exceptionally mild New Year 2021/22
events.summary: A flow of exceptionally mild tropical maritime air from the Azores, with overcast nights keeping minimums high.
observations: UK's warmest New Year's Eve (16.8 °C, Colwyn Bay) and New Year's Day (16.3 °C, St James's Park).
13.2 °C minimum at Chivenor — a UK January record for highest minimum.

events.title: January record: föhn in the Highlands
events.summary: A localised föhn effect in north-west Scotland. The Met Office notes that föhn is the main cause of highly localised winter temperature extremes in Scotland and Wales, rather than the milder south of England.
observations: 19.9 °C at Achfary — 13.0 °C above its January average and 1.6 °C above the previous UK January record.

prolonged-cold-spell.name: Prolonged cold spell
prolonged-cold-spell.summary: Cold weather lasting weeks rather than days, usually because a blocking pattern keeps the Atlantic at bay. Snow lies, little thaws between snowfalls, and frost deepens.
body: From 17 December 2009 to 15 January 2010 the UK had its most widespread and prolonged spell of this type since 1981/82: frequent snow, daytime temperatures often below freezing and little thaw. December 2010 was more severe still. The great historical examples are 1947 and 1962–63; the Met Office describes 1963 as the coldest winter in England and Wales since 1740.
regions: Affects the whole UK; worst in the east and north and inland.

essential: A persistent block diverting Atlantic weather.
Repeated cold air advection from the north or east.

outcomes: Weeks of frost and lying snow.
Freezing of lakes, rivers and harbours in extreme cases.
Snowmelt floods when the thaw comes.

impacts.people: Excess winter mortality.

signals: Persistent blocking in extended-range ensembles
Increases confidence in a long spell.
Breakdowns are hard to time.
prolonged-cold-spell.frequency: Plausible in mid-winter; spells on the scale of 1963 or 2010 are rare.

events.title: Winter of 1947 and the March snowmelt floods
events.summary: High pressure over southern Scandinavia set up a pattern that dominated for weeks. Snow fell somewhere in the UK every day for 55 days. When milder air and Atlantic rain arrived in mid-March, meltwater ran off ground still frozen solid, and rivers across England burst their banks; 70% of houses in Selby were flooded.
observations: Drifts up to seven metres deep in Scotland by 12 March.
Woburn fell to −21 °C on 25 February.
Snow depth of 1.65 m near Ruthin in March 1947 — the deepest recorded in an inhabited area of the UK.

events.title: Winter of 1962–63
events.summary: A high north-east of the British Isles from 22 December dragged bitterly cold winds across the country for most of the winter — the coldest in England and Wales since 1740. Snow covered much of England every day until early March; even sea water froze in some harbours.
observations: Braemar −22.2 °C on 18 January 1963.
Blizzard of 29–30 December with drifts up to 6 m in Wales and south-west England.

events.title: Snow and low temperatures, December 2009 to January 2010
events.summary: The most widespread and prolonged spell of its type since 1981/82: frequent snowfalls with little thaw between them, nights often below −10 °C and below −15 °C in Highland glens.
observations: Depths of 10 to 20 cm widely.

events.title: Snow and low temperatures, December 2010
events.summary: Two spells of severe winter weather. Persistent easterly and north-easterly winds brought bitterly cold air from northern Europe and Siberia; eastern Scotland and north-east England saw the heaviest snow, which then spread so that much of the UK lay under snow by early December.
observations: 50 cm or more on higher ground in eastern Scotland and north-east England.
Below −20 °C on occasion in northern Scotland.
Christmas 2010: snow lying at 83% of stations, the highest ever recorded.

events.title: Prolonged low temperatures, December 2022
events.summary: An Arctic maritime air mass brought hard frosts even in cities and on coasts, with widespread though generally shallow snow. Four children died after falling through the ice on a lake near Solihull.
observations: Braemar −9.3 °C maximum on 12 December — the UK's lowest maximum (excluding mountain sites) since December 2010.
Minimums widely −5 to −10 °C.

mild-to-freezing-transition.name: Sudden transition from mild to freezing
mild-to-freezing-transition.summary: A cold front sweeps mild air away and temperatures plunge within hours. Rain-soaked roads can freeze rapidly; rain can turn to snow on the back edge.
body: Behind a vigorous cold front a mild, wet day can become a freezing night. The Met Office notes the 1947 winter began after a mild start to January with temperatures up to 14 °C. The main hazard is ice: surfaces still wet from the day's rain freeze as temperatures fall, often before roads can be treated.

outcomes: Rapid temperature fall; rain turning to sleet or snow.

rain-on-snow.name: Heavy rain on snow-covered ground
rain-on-snow.summary: Heavy rain falls on a snowpack. Rain and meltwater combine and run off quickly, especially if the ground beneath is frozen, raising flood risk sharply.
body: Snow can hold some rain at first, but once saturated the pack releases water rapidly. Mild, windy, humid air melts snow much faster than sunshine alone. If the soil below is still frozen, almost nothing soaks in. The March 1947 floods followed exactly this: rain and rapid thaw onto frozen ground after weeks of snow.

outcomes: Surface-water flooding where drains are blocked by snow and ice.

snowmelt-flooding.name: Snowmelt flooding
snowmelt-flooding.summary: A rapid thaw of a deep, widespread snow cover releases large volumes of water into rivers. The UK's most extensive snowmelt flood was March 1947.
body: After weeks of snow in 1947, temperatures rose rapidly to about 10 °C in mid-March while the ground was still frozen. Meltwater, with rain and gales from a new Atlantic depression, poured into rivers: the Trent burst its banks at Nottingham, and the Wharfe, Derwent, Aire and Ouse flooded a huge area of southern Yorkshire — about 70% of houses in Selby were flooded. The Met Office describes the autumn 2000 floods as the most extensive since these 1947 snowmelt floods.
regions: Spey and Dee catchments with large snowpacks.
outcomes: Widespread river flooding days after the thaw begins.

UK snowpack monitoring is limited.

Storm Bert (November 2024) was described by the Met Office as a multi-hazard storm with extremely wet and windy weather. Storm Deirdre (December 2018) combined wind, rain, Highland snow and freezing rain.
Multi-hazard storms stretch response services: power repairs may be hindered by snow, flood defences by wind and waves.

winter-thunderstorms.name: Winter thunderstorms, hail showers and thundersnow
winter-thunderstorms.summary: Cold air crossing the relatively warm sea in winter builds cumulonimbus clouds that bring hail, graupel, squalls and lightning — sometimes as thundersnow — mainly to western and northern coasts.
body: The Met Office notes hail is most common in western regions, most frequently in winter, when the land is colder than the sea and showers form over the North Atlantic and Irish Sea. These clouds are shallower than summer storms but can still produce lightning, often a few powerful strikes rather than many.

Thundersnow is the Met Office's term for thunderstorms in wintry conditions producing heavy snow; lightning looks brighter as it reflects off the flakes and thunder is muffled, heard only within 2 to 3 miles.

essential: Cold air aloft over a relatively warm sea.
favourable: Troughs and cold fronts organising showers.

signals: Sea–air temperature contrast and lapse rates

Lightning in winter is often sparse and hard to predict.
winter-thunderstorms.frequency: Plausible through the winter half-year on western coasts.

spring-temperature-swings.name: Rapid alternation between warm and cold days
spring-temperature-swings.summary: Spring air masses differ more than at any other time: a southerly can bring summer warmth one week and an Arctic northerly wintry showers the next.
body: In late March 2021 England and Wales reached 20 to 22 °C widely, with 24.5 °C at Kew; within a week a northerly brought Arctic maritime air, maximums of 6 to 7 °C, wintry showers and hard frosts — a fall of around 15 °C. The Met Office reported several stations recording their lowest April temperature for over 40 years.

The swings happen because continental Europe warms quickly in spring while the Arctic and the surrounding seas remain cold, so the temperature of the air reaching the UK depends heavily on wind direction.
regions: Largest swings away from the moderating sea.

essential: Rapidly changing wind direction between southerly and northerly sources.

outcomes: Warm sunny days followed by wintry showers and frost.
Damage to early growth from frosts after warmth.

impacts.agriculture: Frost damage to blossom and early crops after warm spells encourage growth.

signals: Medium-range ensembles
Large spread in temperature forecasts is typical in spring.
spring-temperature-swings.frequency: Seasonally common in March to May.

body: Spring 2025, the UK's warmest and sunniest on record, was dominated by high pressure building from the Azores or continental Europe, blocking Atlantic fronts. Spring 2011 was the warmest for 100 years at the time, with remarkable warmth in April and persistent lack of rain in March and April, particularly in England and Wales.

sunshine-and-showers.name: Frequent sunshine and scattered showers
sunshine-and-showers.summary: Cool air over sun-warmed ground builds cumulus clouds into showers by afternoon; bright, clear spells come between them.
body: The Met Office explains showers form from convective clouds when air is heated and rises. In spring the sun is strong but the air aloft is still cold, so convection develops readily over land by day, giving the familiar pattern of sunny mornings, showery afternoons and clearing evenings.
outcomes: Short, sharp showers, sometimes with hail.

spring-thunderstorms.name: Spring thunderstorms

monthNotes.may: May 2000: the Bracknell storm brought 65 mm in about an hour and hail up to 1.5 cm.

spring-thunderstorms.summary: As the land warms, showers grow tall enough for thunder. Early in spring they tend to be cold-air storms with hail; by May, warmer, humid plumes can produce stronger storms.
body: Two types dominate. Cold-air storms form in polar maritime air under a cold trough: low-topped, hail-laden, usually brief. Warm-plume storms arrive in May as warm, moist air from the south meets cooler Atlantic air, as in the Bracknell storm of 7 May 2000.

essential: Instability: warm low levels, cold air aloft.
A trigger: heating, a trough or front.

spring-thunderstorms.frequency: Plausible in March and April; seasonally common by May.

events.title: The Bracknell storm
events.summary: A localised storm after the wettest April on record. Hailstones up to 1.5 cm fell with mostly cloud-to-cloud lightning and some intense ground strikes.
observations: 65 mm in about an hour at Beaufort Park — the 1961–90 May average is 56 mm.

cool-wet-spring.summary: Low pressure dominates spring, bringing frequent rain, cool temperatures and little sunshine.

early-drought.name: Early-season drought development

body: Spring is when evaporation starts to exceed rainfall. A dry spring therefore matters more than a dry winter for crops: in 2011 the exceptionally dry spring had adverse effects on agriculture and the environment, part of the 2010–2012 drought. Groundwater-fed rivers respond more slowly and depend more on the preceding winter's rain.

A sea-breeze front can push many miles inland during the afternoon, bringing a sudden drop in temperature and sometimes haar on eastern coasts. multi-day-heatwave.name: Multi-day heatwave
multi-day-heatwave.summary: At least three consecutive days at or above a county-specific temperature threshold — the Met Office definition of a UK heatwave.
body: The Met Office defines a UK heatwave as at least three consecutive days with maximum temperatures meeting or exceeding a threshold that varies by county, calculated from the 1991–2020 climatology of daily maximum temperature on 15 July. It notes heatwaves can be accompanied by high humidity.

August 2020 was one of the most significant heatwaves in southern England in sixty years: over 34 °C somewhere in the south-east for six consecutive days, several tropical nights, then thunderstorms. June 2026 had heatwave conditions somewhere in the UK every day from 16 to 30 June and set a UK June record of 38.0 °C.

hot-plume.name: Hot continental plume ("Spanish plume")
aka: hot continental or tropical air plume
hot-plume.summary: A tongue of very warm air flows north from Iberia. At first it acts as a lid; when cooler air arrives from the west and surface heating builds, intense thunderstorms can break out.
body: The Met Office identifies three main ingredients: very warm air pushing north from the Spanish plateau; cooler air at height advancing from the west with upper troughs or cold fronts; and strong summer sunshine heating the air near the surface. The warm air from Spain forms a layer at height that initially prevents surface air rising; once the surface warms enough to break through, the energy release produces cumulonimbus, lightning, hail, downpours and sometimes gusty winds, occasionally organising into a mesoscale convective system.
Southern and south-eastern England are most at risk. In 17–21 July 2014 successive plumes produced 62,277 lightning strikes across the UK and 45.8 mm in one hour at Norwich Airport.

observations: April, June and April–July each the wettest on record in the England & Wales series from 1766.
Summer 2012 the wettest for the UK since 1912.

events.title: Wainfleet flood
events.summary: A slow-moving front between cooler air to the north-west and warm, moist air over the near continent gave about 2.5 times the June average in three days. The River Steeping burst its banks and around 600 homes in Wainfleet were evacuated.
observations: About 2.5 times the monthly average rainfall from 10 to 12 June in parts of Lincolnshire.

summer-windstorm.name: Summer windstorm
summer-windstorm.summary: A deep low in summer. Gusts are usually lower than in winter storms, but trees in full leaf, busy campsites, festivals and coastal holidaymakers make impacts disproportionate.
body: Storms Ellen and Francis (August 2020) were two of the most notable August storms in 50 years; trees in full leaf came down on saturated ground. Storm Evert (July 2021) flattened tents on busy campsites; Storm Floris (August 2025) equalled Scotland's August gust record of 82 mph at Wick; Storm Hector (June 2018) came after weeks of settled weather.
regions: Holiday areas exposed to Atlantic lows.

essential: A deep low and strong jet in summer.

impacts.people: Danger at campsites, beaches and festivals.
impacts.transport: Rail and road disruption.

safety: Camping in wind and rain advice.

events.title: Summer storm, 7–8 July 2004
events.summary: A depression from Spain and France brought unseasonably high winds and heavy rain, followed by thunderstorms.
observations: Over 100 mm in 18 hours at Wittering — double its July 1961–90 average.

events.title: Storm Hector
events.summary: Unseasonably strong winds after weeks of largely fine, settled weather.
observations: A few gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) in Northern Ireland, North Wales and northern England.

events.title: Storms Ellen and Francis
events.summary: A strong jet stream drove deep lows across the UK in late August: two of the most notable August storms of the last 50 years. Trees in full leaf on saturated ground came down; beach huts at Woolacombe were washed away.
observations: 69 knots (79 mph) at Capel Curig (Ellen); 70 knots (81 mph) at Needles Old Battery (Francis).

events.title: Storm Evert
events.summary: Unusually strong winds for the time of year flattened tents on busy holiday campsites.
observations: 67 knots (77 mph) at Needles Old Battery.

events.title: Storm Floris
events.summary: One of the most severe summer wind storms to affect Scotland in the observational record. The East Coast Main Line closed north of Newcastle and over 70,000 properties lost power.
observations: Gust of 71 knots (82 mph) at Wick Airport, equalling Scotland's August gust record.

thundery-breakdown.name: Heat followed by a sharp cold front and thunderstorms
thundery-breakdown.summary: A hot spell ends as a cold front or trough arrives. Storms erupt along and ahead of it, bringing torrential rain, hail, lightning and gusts, before fresher air follows.
body: The Northern Ireland record heat of July 2021 ended in a thundery breakdown with flash flooding in south-east England that closed sections of the M11. In August 2020 a line of severe thunderstorms crossed north-east Scotland while southern England was at 34–35 °C. The 1 July 2015 heat also triggered thunderstorms in northern England and Scotland.
regions: Wherever the front meets the heat.

essential: An approaching cold front or upper trough.

thundery-breakdown.frequency: Common at the end of summer hot spells.

events.title: One-day heatwave, 1 July 2015
events.summary: Hot air from Spain set a new July record; the heat also triggered thunderstorms in northern England and Scotland.
observations: 36.7 °C at Heathrow.

events.title: September 2016 heat and storms
events.summary: A southerly flow from France and Spain brought exceptional heat; humidity fed thunderstorms with flash flooding.
observations: 34.4 °C at Gravesend — the highest September temperature since 1911.
Several hourly totals over 30 mm.

events.title: August 2020 heatwave
events.summary: Hot, humid air from the near continent: one of the most significant heatwaves in southern England in sixty years. Thunderstorms brought hail, lightning fires and flash flooding that closed part of the M25.
observations: Over 34 °C somewhere in the south-east for six consecutive days.
Several tropical nights above 20 °C.

events.title: North-east Scotland thunderstorms
events.summary: A line of severe thunderstorms crossed north-east Scotland while southern England baked at 34 to 35 °C. The torrential rain seems likely to have been a factor in the landslip that derailed a train at Stonehaven, killing three people.
observations: 30 to 50 mm or more within three hours in places.

events.title: Northern Ireland temperature record
events.summary: A week of heat in the west. The Met Office issued the UK's first extreme heat warning. The spell ended in a thundery breakdown with flash flooding in south-east England.
observations: 31.3 °C at Castlederg, County Tyrone, on 21 July — the all-time Northern Ireland record.

autumn-warmth.name: Late-season warmth (autumn summer-like spells)
autumn-warmth.summary: A warm, settled spell in September, October or even November. Warm autumn spells are not uncommon, and there is no evidence that they recur at particular dates.
body: The Met Office does not use the expression "Indian summer" itself, noting its uncertain origins; its 1916 glossary defined it as "a warm, calm spell of weather occurring in autumn, especially in October and November". It also points out there is no statistical evidence that such spells recur at any particular time each year.
The warmest UK temperatures recorded in October and November are 29.9 °C (Gravesend, 1 October 2011) and 22.4 °C (Trawsgoed, 1 November 2015).
regions: Warm in the lee of fronts (Storm Callum, October 2018).

essential: High pressure or a warm southerly flow.

outcomes: Warm, sunny afternoons; misty, cool mornings.
autumn-warmth.frequency: Common in September; plausible in October and November.

stats.text: UK October record 29.9 °C (Gravesend, 1 October 2011); November record 22.4 °C (Trawsgoed, 1 November 2015).

events.title: September 2023 heatwave
events.summary: Over 30 °C somewhere in the UK for seven consecutive days — the longest such September run on record. 10 September was, unusually, the hottest day of the year.
observations: 33.5 °C at Faversham, Kent, on 10 September.
Northern Ireland September record 28.0 °C at Castlederg.

late-heatwave.name: Residual (late-season) heatwave
late-heatwave.summary: Heatwave conditions in late August or September, when the sun is weaker but the land and sea are at their warmest.
body: September 2023 had over 30 °C somewhere in the UK for seven consecutive days — the longest such September run on record — and 33.5 °C at Faversham made 10 September the hottest day of that year. September 2016 reached 34.4 °C at Gravesend, the highest September temperature since 1911, with flash-flooding thunderstorms.
regions: Northern Ireland set a September record of 28.0 °C in 2023.

essential: High pressure and a warm continental source.

outcomes: Heat stress, especially as schools return.
safety: Hot-weather advice applies in September too.

ex-tropical-cyclone.name: Ex-tropical or post-tropical cyclone
ex-tropical-cyclone.summary: The remains of an Atlantic hurricane or tropical storm, transformed into a mid-latitude storm, reach the UK — usually in late summer or autumn, when the hurricane season peaks.
body: By the time they reach the UK, these systems are no longer hurricanes: they have lost their tropical structure and often re-intensify as ordinary Atlantic lows, sometimes carrying very moist tropical air. Ex-hurricane Ophelia (16 October 2017) brought gusts of 60–70 knots to exposed Irish Sea coasts and three deaths in Ireland. Ex-Bertha (August 2014) gave north-east Scotland double its August rainfall. Lorenzo (October 2019) weakened rapidly and had limited UK impacts.
The 1987 Great Storm was not a hurricane: the Met Office points out it did not originate in the tropics.
regions: Often on or near the track.

essential: A tropical cyclone recurving into the North Atlantic.

signals: National Hurricane Center tracks plus UK model forecasts
Show whether a system will recurve towards the UK.
Extratropical transition is notoriously hard to forecast.
ex-tropical-cyclone.frequency: Plausible in late August to October.

events.title: Ex-hurricane Bertha
events.summary: The remnants of Bertha brought unseasonably windy and very wet weather. North-east Scotland was worst hit: 200 homes were evacuated in Elgin.
observations: Some places in north-east Scotland had double the August average rainfall.

events.title: Ex-hurricane Ophelia
events.summary: On the 30th anniversary of the Great Storm, ex-Ophelia brought very strong winds to western Britain and Ireland, where three people died. Thousands of homes in Wales and Northern Ireland lost power.
observations: Gusts of 60 to 70 knots or higher on exposed Irish Sea coasts, especially west Wales.

events.title: Storm Lorenzo
events.summary: A mid-Atlantic hurricane weakened rapidly as it tracked past the Azores towards Ireland. Limited impacts across the UK.
observations: Mainly affected the west of Ireland.

tropical-moisture-interaction.name: Tropical remnants interacting with Atlantic weather
tropical-moisture-interaction.summary: A tropical system does not itself reach the UK, but its moisture and energy feed into an Atlantic low or front, intensifying it.
body: Storm Agnes (September 2023) was an intense low enhanced by energy from Tropical Storm Ophelia, which had affected the US east coast; Agnes weakened before reaching the UK but still produced the equal-highest September gust for Wales (73 knots at Capel Curig). Moisture drawn from tropical systems can also feed atmospheric rivers.

essential: A tropical system or its moisture interacting with the North Atlantic jet.

outcomes: Heavier rain than the parent low alone would give.
signals: Moisture transport forecasts
Track tropical moisture into mid-latitude systems.
Highly uncertain beyond a few days.
tropical-moisture-interaction.frequency: Plausible in late summer and autumn.

events.title: Storm Agnes
events.summary: An intense low enhanced by energy from Tropical Storm Ophelia, weakening before it reached the UK. Impacts were relatively modest overall.
observations: 73 knots (84 mph) at Capel Curig — the equal-highest September gust for Wales.

early-cold-snap.name: Early cold snap

monthNotes.oct: Late October 2008 set record October lows and brought snow to parts of south-east England.

early-cold-snap.summary: A northerly brings the first taste of winter in autumn: frosts, hail and, on northern hills, the first snow.
body: In late October 2008 some stations set new October records for low maximum and minimum temperatures, and snow was recorded at Reading, Hampstead and Odiham in the climate district of SE and Central S England — unusual so early.

essential: A northerly outbreak of polar or Arctic air.

early-cold-snap.frequency: Plausible in October and November; uncommon in September.

events.title: October snow in south-east England
events.summary: Record low October temperatures and snow. Reading, Hampstead and Odiham recorded a day of snow — unusual for the climate district in October.
observations: Some stations set new October records for low maximum and minimum temperatures.

first-frosts.name: First widespread frosts
first-frosts.summary: Lengthening nights under clear skies bring the first air frosts, usually in sheltered rural areas in October and more widely in November.
body: The UK area-average number of air-frost days rises from 0.1 in September to 1.6 in October and 5.5 in November (1991–2020). Frost arrives first in sheltered inland valleys and glens, and last on coasts and islands.
outcomes: Ground and air frost at dawn.

stats.text: UK area-average days of air frost: September 0.1, October 1.6, November 5.5.

autumn-thunderstorms.name: Autumn thunderstorms and hail
autumn-thunderstorms.summary: As cold air arrives over seas still warm from summer, showers and thunderstorms develop, especially near western and southern coasts and along fronts.
body: The sea is at its warmest relative to the air in autumn, which fuels convection near coasts. The Ottery St Mary hailstorm (29–30 October 2008) formed on an unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow lifted over Woodbury Common: about two hours of hail left banks up to 1.2 m deep.

essential: A trigger: front, trough or hills.

outcomes: Hail, thunder and squalls near coasts.
autumn-thunderstorms.frequency: Plausible in September; common on western coasts in October and November.

events.title: Ottery St Mary hailstorm
events.summary: An unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow forced up over Woodbury Common, produced about two hours of hail. The hailstones were small, but hail banks reached 1.2 m deep and blocked drains; about 100 people were evacuated.
observations: 187 mm in 27 hours at King's School; an estimated 160 mm in three hours (return period over 200 years).

autumn-abrupt-transition.name: Abrupt switch from warm weather to cold and wet
autumn-abrupt-transition.summary: A late-summer warm spell ends suddenly as the first autumn storm sweeps in: temperatures drop sharply, wind and rain arrive together.
body: The Met Office described storms Ali and Bronagh (September 2018) as marking an emphatic transition from the fine summer of 2018 to autumn, and Storm Alex (October 2020) as an emphatic transition to unsettled autumnal weather.

essential: A strengthening jet ending a settled spell.

sourceRecords.title: Strong winds and heavy rain from storms Ali and Bronagh
Storm Alex and heavy rain 2 to 4 October 2020

autumn-anticyclone.name: Prolonged settled autumn high pressure
autumn-anticyclone.summary: High pressure holds the Atlantic back for weeks: calm, dry days, sunshine or gloom, and increasingly long foggy nights.
body: Autumn does not guarantee storms. When high pressure dominates, days can be mild and sunny, nights foggy and increasingly frosty. Such autumns can still contain one severe event if the pattern breaks — which is why the absence of storms in one month says little about the next.

essential: A persistent high over or near the UK.

autumn-anticyclone.frequency: Common in September; plausible in October and November.

dry-autumn.name: Dry autumn
aka: agricultural impacts of a dry autumn
dry-autumn.summary: Autumn rain fails, so soils and groundwater do not recover after summer. Water resources go into winter in deficit and autumn-sown crops struggle to establish.
body: Autumn is when soils normally re-wet and groundwater begins to recharge. The 2010–2012 drought developed through a sequence of dry months, particularly in spring, autumn and winter. In 2003 August and September were exceptionally dry in many areas and October also below average, before heavy rain fell over south-east England on 20–23 November.

essential: Persistent high pressure or a jet far to the north in autumn.

events.title: Warm, dry and sunny 2003
events.summary: The warmest year in the UK series at the time; August and September were exceptionally dry in many areas, and November brought double the average in parts of the south-east after a dry summer and autumn.
observations: UK 2003: warmest, third driest and second sunniest year in the series from 1961.

widespread-frontal-rain.name: Widespread frontal rain
widespread-frontal-rain.summary: A broad band of rain associated with a warm front, cold front or occlusion crosses the country, giving hours of steady, sometimes heavy, rain.
body: The Met Office explains that fronts mark the boundaries between warm and cold air; warm air is lifted along them, producing extensive cloud and rain. Warm fronts typically bring steady rain spreading in over several hours; cold fronts a narrower, heavier band with a sudden wind change; occlusions a mixture.

Most frontal rain is unremarkable, but a widespread, slow band can give exceptional totals across a large area: on 3 October 2020 the UK area-average rainfall was 31.7 mm, the UK's wettest day in a series back to 1891.

essential: A frontal system crossing the UK.

outcomes: Local surface-water flooding where it is heavy.
signals: Front positions on charts and radar
Track timing.
Embedded heavier bursts are hard to place.

events.title: Storm Alex and the UK's wettest day
events.summary: Alex marked an emphatic transition to unsettled autumn weather; associated fronts brought prolonged, widespread heavy rain on 3–4 October.
observations: UK area-average 31.7 mm on 3 October 2020 — the UK's wettest day on record in a daily series back to 1891.

sourceRecords.title: Storm Alex and heavy rain 2 to 4 October 2020

orographic-rain.name: Persistent orographic rainfall over western uplands
orographic-rain.summary: Moist air forced up mountains cools, and its water vapour condenses into heavy, persistent rain on the windward slopes — the reason the Lake District, Snowdonia and the western Highlands are the UK's wettest places.
body: When a moist south-westerly meets the western hills, rising air cools and rainfall is greatly increased: the Met Office describes the October 2021 Cumbrian event as a "warm-conveyor" where rainfall was greatly increased over high ground as moist air was forced to rise. The UK's 24-hour, 2-day, 3-day and 4-day rainfall records are all held by Cumbrian sites in such events.
On the lee side, descending air warms and dries, creating rain shadows: the Met Office notes the west may be wet while the lower-lying east enjoys warmth and sunshine.
regions: Lake District fells hold UK rainfall records.

favourable: A slow-moving or stalled front in the flow.

outcomes: Very large rain totals on windward slopes over 24–72 hours.
Rain shadow and föhn warmth to the lee.

impacts.rivers: Major river flooding in Cumbria, Wales and Scotland.
impacts.transport: Landslips on mountain roads (A83 Rest and Be Thankful).

signals: Moisture transport and wind direction relative to hills
Identify where uplift will be strongest.
Totals on summits are poorly observed.
orographic-rain.frequency: Common in western uplands through the autumn and winter.

stats.text: UK 24-hour record 341.4 mm (Honister Pass, 4–5 Dec 2015); 2-day 405.0 mm (Thirlmere, 2015); 3-day 456.4 mm and 4-day 495.0 mm (Seathwaite, November 2009).

climate.observed: Heavy rainfall events have become more intense in the UK.
climate.projected: Further increases in winter rainfall and the intensity of heavy rain are projected.

safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.
Know the three flood warning levels: Flood Alert, Flood Warning and Severe Flood Warning (danger to life).

events.title: Carlisle floods
events.summary: Prolonged rain over the Lake District and Pennines drained into the River Eden. Three people were killed; it was the worst flood in Carlisle since 1822.
observations: A near-stationary front in a westerly airstream, followed by a very deep depression.

events.title: Lake District floods
events.summary: Exceptionally prolonged heavy rain on ground that had already had close to the whole-month November average. Many Lake District rivers exceeded their previous maximum flows by a wide margin.
observations: Over 400 mm on some high ground in 72 hours.
316 mm in 24 hours at Seathwaite.

events.title: Storm Desmond and the Cumbria floods
events.summary: Exceptional rain over the Cumbrian fells fell on ground already saturated by a very wet November, causing widespread flooding — following Carlisle 2005 and Cumbria 2009.
observations: 341.4 mm at Honister Pass in 24 hours to 1800 GMT on 5 December — the UK 24-hour record.
405.0 mm at Thirlmere over two rain-days — the UK 2-day record.

events.title: Storm Callum
events.summary: One of the most significant extreme rainfall and flood events in south Wales in 50 years. The front also produced a temperature contrast of more than 10 °C, with unseasonable warmth in eastern England.
observations: 100 to 150 mm over much of the Brecon Beacons in two days, up to 200 mm on high ground.

events.title: Storm Ciara
events.summary: The most significant storm for gust speeds across England and Wales overall since 12 February 2014, with persistent heavy rain over the uplands of north-west England. The Humber Bridge closed for only the second time in its history.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots widely across England and Wales.
Over a month's rain in about 18 hours in parts of West Yorkshire.

events.title: Storm Dennis
events.summary: A week after Ciara, Dennis brought 50 to 100 mm or more to western uplands on saturated ground. A red warning for rain covered parts of south Wales; the Wye and Severn were reported at their highest-ever levels and over 1,400 homes and businesses flooded.
observations: Over 600 flood warnings and alerts from the Environment Agency.

events.title: Storm Christoph
events.summary: One of the wettest 3-day periods on record for north-west England and North Wales. As the storm cleared it brought significant snow and blizzards over the north-east uplands. Much of Northwich town centre was under water.
observations: 100 mm or more over upland areas.

events.title: Heavy and persistent rain, October 2021
events.summary: A slow-moving front produced a 'warm-conveyor' event, very similar to December 2015 and November 2009. About 40 properties flooded, while over 1,200 were protected by defences.
observations: Over 400 mm on the Lake District fells in six days.
Two gauges recorded daily totals over 200 mm on the 27th.

events.title: Atmospheric river over Scotland
events.summary: A narrow stream of moisture-laden air gave the wettest 2-day period on record for Scotland, while England and Wales reached the low 20s °C on the warm side of the front. Ten people were airlifted from their vehicles when a landslip closed the A83.
observations: 100 to 150 mm widely over the Southern and Central Highlands.
25 °C in parts of south-east England at the same time.

events.title: Storm Bert
events.summary: A multi-hazard storm with extremely wet and windy weather; over 150 mm on the wettest uplands of South Wales and south-west England, with gusts over 60 knots even at some inland locations.
observations: 23 November was the UK's wettest day as an area average since 3 October 2020.

events.title: Storm Darragh
events.summary: A red warning for wind covered West Wales and both coasts of the Bristol Channel. Two weeks after storm Bert, a further 50 to 100 mm fell over upland Wales.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots or higher in the red-warning area.
Broadly comparable with Isha, slightly less severe than Eunice; 12 February 2014 was much more severe.

atmospheric-river.name: Atmospheric river
atmospheric-river.summary: A long, narrow stream of very moist air that can carry huge quantities of water vapour from the subtropics. Where it meets hills or stalls, it can produce extreme rainfall.
body: The Met Office described the record Scottish rainfall of 6–7 October 2023 as due to an atmospheric river, a narrow stream of moisture-laden air capable of causing very high rainfall totals: 100 to 150 mm widely across the Southern and Central Highlands, the wettest 2-day period on record for Scotland.
Atmospheric rivers feed the warm conveyor of Atlantic lows. Their impact depends on whether they move through quickly or stall over the same hills.

essential: A concentrated plume of moisture transport from the subtropics.
favourable: Stalling against high ground or a blocking pattern.

outcomes: Warm, humid conditions on the warm side.
signals: Integrated vapour transport (IVT) forecasts
Identify atmospheric rivers days ahead.
Exact landfall and duration vary.
atmospheric-river.frequency: Common in autumn; plausible in winter.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.

slow-moving-front.name: Slow-moving rain-bearing weather system
slow-moving-front.summary: A front slows down or stalls across the UK, so rain falls on the same areas for many hours — often on the boundary between much warmer and colder air.
body: On 7 November 2019 a slow-moving front gave 50–100 mm in a swathe from the Humber to Sheffield — around the whole-month average or more in 24 hours — causing severe flooding from the Derwent and Don. On 25–26 October 2019 a slow-moving front from South Wales to Lincolnshire separated 7 °C in Birmingham from 17 °C in London. The Easter 1998 floods came from a stationary band of heavy rain over the Midlands.

essential: A front with little forward motion.
favourable: A large temperature contrast across it.

outcomes: Prolonged heavy rain in a band.
Sharp temperature contrast across the front.
signals: Model rainfall accumulations
Highlight swathes of large totals.
Exact position of the swathe is uncertain by tens of km.
slow-moving-front.frequency: Common in autumn; plausible all year.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.
Know the three flood warning levels: Flood Alert, Flood Warning and Severe Flood Warning (danger to life).

events.title: Easter 1998 floods
events.summary: A stationary band of heavy rain over the Midlands caused floods in which five people died and thousands were evacuated. In many rivers flood levels were higher than the record 1947 flood.
observations: Over 75 mm from Worcestershire towards The Wash.
Over 4,200 homes and businesses flooded in England and Wales.

events.title: Cambridge record daily rain
events.summary: A slow-moving front over eastern England.
observations: 90.4 mm in 18 hours at Cambridge Guildhall — the highest 24-hour total at the Cambridge sites since 1900 (Met Office estimate: 140-year return period).

events.title: South Yorkshire floods
events.summary: A slow-moving front gave around a whole month's rain in 24 hours on catchments already saturated since late September. The Derwent and Don flooded severely; about 500 homes flooded around Doncaster.

events.summary: A blocking high over Scandinavia held the system in place, bringing exceptional rain to eastern Scotland (two red warnings for rain) and heavy, widespread rain across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

events.title: Exceptionally wet weather, May 2024
events.summary: A slow-moving front around a low off the east coast. A schoolgirl died in a mudslide in North Yorkshire and the West Coast Main Line closed.

rain-on-saturated-ground.name: Prolonged rain over saturated ground
rain-on-saturated-ground.summary: After weeks of rain the ground can absorb no more, so even ordinary rainfall runs off straight into rivers. Many of the UK's worst floods follow this pattern rather than one extreme downpour.
body: The Met Office repeatedly identifies antecedent wetness as a key factor: Storm Dennis's 50–100 mm fell on saturated ground after Ciara; the November 2012 events were individually unexceptional but their succession on saturated ground caused widespread flooding; Cumbria's December 2015 floods were exacerbated by already very wet ground after storm Desmond and a very wet November.
regions: Any catchment after a wet spell.
signals: Soil-moisture deficit and river levels
Show how primed catchments are.
Catchment response varies.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.
Know the three flood warning levels: Flood Alert, Flood Warning and Severe Flood Warning (danger to life).

events.title: Storm Desmond and the Cumbria floods
events.summary: Exceptional rain over the Cumbrian fells fell on ground already saturated by a very wet November, causing widespread flooding — following Carlisle 2005 and Cumbria 2009.

events.title: South Yorkshire floods
events.summary: A slow-moving front gave around a whole month's rain in 24 hours on catchments already saturated since late September. The Derwent and Don flooded severely; about 500 homes flooded around Doncaster.
observations: 50 to 100 mm from the Humber to Sheffield in 24 hours.

events.title: Storm Dennis
events.summary: A week after Ciara, Dennis brought 50 to 100 mm or more to western uplands on saturated ground. A red warning for rain covered parts of south Wales; the Wye and Severn were reported at their highest-ever levels and over 1,400 homes and businesses flooded.
observations: Over 600 flood warnings and alerts from the Environment Agency.

events.title: Storm Babet

events.title: Storm Claudia
events.summary: Parts of England and Wales had the whole-month November average in six days. A major incident was declared in Monmouth as the River Monnow flooded; over 50 properties flooded and 18,000 were protected by defences.

intense-convective-rain.name: Intense convective rainfall
intense-convective-rain.summary: Rain from cumulonimbus clouds falls at extreme rates — tens of millimetres in an hour — over small areas, overwhelming drains and small streams.
body: Convective rain is short and localised but intense. In July 2019, 40 to 60 mm fell in one hour in parts of North Yorkshire. The UK 60-minute record is 92 mm (Maidenhead, 12 July 1901) and the 30-minute record 80 mm (Eskdalemuir, 26 June 1953).
Totals depend as much on how long a storm stays over one place as on its intensity.

favourable: Repeated development over the same area.

outcomes: Flash flooding of roads and properties.
signals: Radar rainfall rates and storm motion
Nowcast intense rain.
Little lead time.

stats.text: UK short-duration records: 30 min 80 mm (Eskdalemuir, 1953); 60 min 92 mm (Maidenhead, 1901); 180 min 178 mm (Horncastle, 1960).

safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.

events.title: The Bracknell storm
events.summary: A localised storm after the wettest April on record. Hailstones up to 1.5 cm fell with mostly cloud-to-cloud lightning and some intense ground strikes.
observations: 65 mm in about an hour at Beaufort Park — the 1961–90 May average is 56 mm.
Estimated by the Met Office as a 1 in 112 year event.

events.title: Spanish plume events, July 2014
events.summary: Successive plumes of very warm, humid air from Iberia and France were overrun by cooler air aloft, giving several outbreaks of intense thunderstorms.
observations: 62,277 lightning strikes from 17 to 21 July.
45.8 mm in one hour at Norwich Airport on 20 July.

events.title: Yorkshire Dales flash floods and Whaley Bridge
events.summary: Thunderstorms caused flash flooding in Swaledale and Arkengarthdale: a bridge collapsed near Grinton. The next day, damage to the spillway of Toddbrook Reservoir led to thousands being evacuated from Whaley Bridge.
observations: 40 to 60 mm in one hour in parts of North Yorkshire; 60 to 80 mm or more in two hours.

events.title: Extreme Norfolk rainfall
events.summary: Thunderstorms gave a remarkable daily total at East Wretham. Flood impacts were relatively modest because the extreme rain was very localised, in a rural, low-lying area — a reminder that rainfall amount and flood impact are not the same thing.
observations: 239.9 mm at East Wretham — a new UK August daily record for an individual station.

flash-flooding.name: Localised flash flooding
flash-flooding.summary: Water levels rise within minutes to a couple of hours after intense rain, often in steep, small catchments or urban areas — leaving little time to react.
body: At Boscastle on 16 August 2004 about 75 mm fell in two hours; two rivers burst their banks and about two billion litres of water rushed through the village. Local topography made the flood worse. In July 2019 flash floods in Swaledale collapsed a bridge near Grinton.

Flash flooding is not just a summer hazard: an intense line of rain flooded parts of Cornwall in November 2010, and the Ottery St Mary hailstorm in October 2008 caused flash flooding when hail blocked drains.
regions: Steep, short catchments near the coast.
outcomes: Sudden, fast-flowing water in streets and valleys.
Debris, damaged bridges, cars swept away.

impacts.people: Danger to life with little warning.

signals: Nowcasting with radar

Lead times of minutes to an hour.

flash-flooding.frequency: Common somewhere in the UK in summer; plausible in other seasons.

events.title: Boscastle flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours formed bands aligned with the wind, holding heavy rain over north Cornwall for hours. Coastal wind convergence and high ground triggered the storms and the local topography concentrated the flood. Around 75 mm fell in two hours; two rivers burst their banks and about two billion litres of water rushed through the village. Nobody died, thanks largely to a huge helicopter rescue.
observations: About 75 mm in two hours — the normal August total.
Comparable past events listed by the Met Office: Martinstown 1955 (279.4 mm in 24 h), Lynmouth 1952 (229.5 mm in 24 h).

events.title: North York Moors flash flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours spread from north-west England across North Yorkshire; Helmsley was among the places flooded.
observations: Just over 50 mm in 30 minutes at Hawnby.
Return periods over 200 years for 30-minute, 1-hour and 3-hour totals (Flood Estimation Handbook method).

events.title: Ottery St Mary hailstorm
events.summary: An unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow forced up over Woodbury Common, produced about two hours of hail. The hailstones were small, but hail banks reached 1.2 m deep and blocked drains; about 100 people were evacuated.
observations: 187 mm in 27 hours at King's School; an estimated 160 mm in three hours (return period over 200 years).

events.title: Cornwall floods
events.summary: A line of intense rain developed with a deep autumn low, flooding St Blazey, St Austell, Mevagissey and Lostwithiel. More than 100 properties flooded and the main line to Penzance closed.
observations: 40 mm or more in two hours in places.

events.title: Yorkshire Dales flash floods and Whaley Bridge
events.summary: Thunderstorms caused flash flooding in Swaledale and Arkengarthdale: a bridge collapsed near Grinton. The next day, damage to the spillway of Toddbrook Reservoir led to thousands being evacuated from Whaley Bridge.
observations: 40 to 60 mm in one hour in parts of North Yorkshire; 60 to 80 mm or more in two hours.

events.title: North-east Scotland thunderstorms
events.summary: A line of severe thunderstorms crossed north-east Scotland while southern England baked at 34 to 35 °C. The torrential rain seems likely to have been a factor in the landslip that derailed a train at Stonehaven, killing three people.
observations: 30 to 50 mm or more within three hours in places.

river-flooding.name: River flooding after prolonged rain
river-flooding.summary: Rivers overtop their banks as rain over a whole catchment, often over days or weeks, exceeds what the channel can carry. Large rivers may peak days after the rain stops.
body: River flooding depends on the catchment as well as the rainfall. Large rivers such as the Severn and Thames respond slowly and stay high for long periods; small upland rivers respond within hours. Storm Dennis (February 2020) brought the Wye and Severn to what were reported as their highest-ever levels; the autumn 2000 floods affected 10,000 homes and businesses at 700 locations.
outcomes: Flooding of riverside property and farmland.
Peak flows lagging rainfall by hours to days.

events.title: Rain, wind and Pennine snow, New Year 2024–25

surface-water-flooding.name: Surface-water flooding after intense rain
surface-water-flooding.summary: Rain falls faster than drains and the ground can take it, so water ponds and flows over the surface before it ever reaches a river.
body: Surface-water flooding can occur far from any river, wherever intense rain meets hard surfaces, blocked drains or baked ground. Thunderstorms closed part of the M25 in August 2020; torrential rain flooded parts of London overnight on 22–23 June 2026; late September 2024 storms flooded several hundred properties in Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire and Oxfordshire.
surface-water-flooding.frequency: Common in summer thunderstorms; plausible all year.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.
Know the three flood warning levels: Flood Alert, Flood Warning and Severe Flood Warning (danger to life).

events.summary: A series of lows in a south-easterly flow of unstable air brought thunderstorms and torrential rain; several hundred properties flooded across Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire and Oxfordshire.
observations: Oxfordshire and Bedfordshire recorded their wettest calendar month on record (series from 1836).

urban-flooding.name: Urban flooding
urban-flooding.summary: Towns and cities flood quickly because water cannot soak into concrete and tarmac, and drainage systems have finite capacity.
body: Urban areas combine the fastest run-off with the most people and infrastructure. Even moderate rainfall rates can flood underpasses and Underground stations; in September 2024 thunderstorms caused disruption on the London Underground. Urban rivers in culverts can also back up.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.
Know the three flood warning levels: Flood Alert, Flood Warning and Severe Flood Warning (danger to life).

groundwater-flooding.name: Groundwater flooding
groundwater-flooding.summary: After a very wet autumn and winter, water tables in chalk and limestone rise to the surface, flooding low ground for weeks or months — often long after the rain has stopped.
body: In the wet winter of 2013–14 and the wet early winter of 2023 (when the Met Office noted an ongoing risk of groundwater flooding during storms Elin and Fergus), saturated aquifers kept springs and valleys flowing. February 2001 followed the record wet autumn of 2000: full aquifers and saturated soils left nowhere for the rain to go but into rivers.

essential: Months of above-average rainfall over permeable rocks.

groundwater-flooding.frequency: Common after very wet winters; otherwise uncommon.

coastal-flooding.name: Coastal flooding from storm surges
aka: combined high tides, strong winds and low pressure
coastal-flooding.summary: The sea floods coastal land when a storm surge, large waves and a high tide coincide. Timing is critical: a couple of hours can decide whether defences are overtopped.
body: The Met Office stresses that in areas with large tides, such as the UK, a couple of hours' difference in the timing of a storm surge can mean the difference between flooding and staying safe. During Storm Eunice severe coastal flooding in the Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary was avoided because the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in places. On 5 December 2013 a surge 2 m above predicted high water coincided with high tide on North Sea coasts.
In March 2008 strong winds, low pressure and a high tide combined to bring coastal flooding to parts of the south coast.

essential: Storm surge from wind and low pressure.

outcomes: Overtopping or breaching of sea defences.
signals: Surge forecasts
Combined with tide tables give expected water levels.
Wave overtopping is very local.
coastal-flooding.frequency: Plausible in autumn and winter storms on exposed, low-lying coasts; major events are uncommon to rare.

events.title: The 1953 North Sea flood
events.summary: A storm in the North Sea drove a surge that coincided with a high spring tide. More than 2,500 people died around the North Sea, including 307 in England and 19 in Scotland. Investment in defences such as the Thames Barrier, and in warning systems, followed.
observations: The greatest storm surge on record in the North Sea (Met Office, Storm Arwen report).
About 160,000 hectares of eastern England flooded.

events.summary: A deep low crossed southern Ireland, Wales and Lincolnshire. Strong winds, low pressure and a high tide combined to bring coastal flooding to parts of the south coast.

rain-on-frozen-ground.name: Rain falling onto frozen ground
rain-on-frozen-ground.summary: After a hard freeze, rain arrives with milder air. Frozen soil cannot absorb it, so water runs off as if over concrete; surfaces may also glaze with ice.
body: In March 1947 the Met Office describes the ground as still frozen solid after weeks of cold weather, leaving the melting snow and rain with nowhere to go — the origin of the widespread snowmelt floods. On a smaller scale, rain on frozen ground often brings ice on untreated surfaces before the thaw takes hold.
rain-on-frozen-ground.frequency: Plausible at the end of cold spells.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.

events.title: Winter of 1947 and the March snowmelt floods
events.summary: High pressure over southern Scandinavia set up a pattern that dominated for weeks. Snow fell somewhere in the UK every day for 55 days. When milder air and Atlantic rain arrived in mid-March, meltwater ran off ground still frozen solid, and rivers across England burst their banks; 70% of houses in Selby were flooded.
observations: Drifts up to seven metres deep in Scotland by 12 March.
Woburn fell to −21 °C on 25 February.
Snow depth of 1.65 m near Ruthin in March 1947 — the deepest recorded in an inhabited area of the UK.

upland-catchment-flooding.name: Rainfall on saturated upland catchments
upland-catchment-flooding.summary: Steep upland catchments with thin soils respond within hours to heavy rain, sending sudden floods down valleys into towns below.
body: In November 2009 many Lake District rivers exceeded their previous maximum flows by a wide margin after over 400 mm fell on some high ground in 72 hours. In June 2005 just over 50 mm fell in 30 minutes at Hawnby on the North York Moors, with return periods over 200 years. Mountain rescue teams advise walkers that streams can become impassable quickly.

essential: Heavy rain on steep, thin-soiled catchments.

outcomes: Rapid river rises; dangerous fords and streams.
safety: It is not safe to drive, walk or swim through floodwater. If you are affected by fast-flowing or deep water, call 999 and wait for help.

multi-day-flood-episode.name: Multi-day flooding episode
multi-day-flood-episode.summary: Flooding that continues or recurs over days or weeks, as successive rain events keep rivers high and catchments saturated.
body: Winter 2013–14 brought months of flooding on the Somerset Levels and along the Thames. December 2015 — the UK's wettest calendar month in a series from 1910 — produced repeated flooding across northern Britain. Summer 2007 showed this can happen in summer too.
regions: Any region under a persistent storm track.
multi-day-flood-episode.frequency: Plausible in wet autumns and winters; uncommon in summer.

events.summary: Exceptional rain over the Cumbrian fells fell on ground already saturated by a very wet November, causing widespread flooding — following Carlisle 2005 and Cumbria 2009.
observations: 341.4 mm at Honister Pass in 24 hours to 1800 GMT on 5 December — the UK 24-hour record.
405.0 mm at Thirlmere over two rain-days — the UK 2-day record.

events.title: Wettest calendar month on record, December 2015
events.summary: A persistent, exceptionally mild south-westerly flow of tropical maritime air brought a series of Atlantic lows, including storms Eva and Frank. Boxing Day rain flooded parts of Lancashire, north Manchester and West Yorkshire.
observations: December 2015 was the wettest calendar month for the UK in a series from 1910.
Also easily the mildest December in the UK series from 1910 and the Central England Temperature series from 1659.

events.title: Storm Babet
events.summary: A blocking high over Scandinavia held the system in place, bringing exceptional rain to eastern Scotland (two red warnings for rain) and heavy, widespread rain across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
observations: 150 to 200 mm in the wettest parts of eastern Scotland.
For Angus, 19 October 2023 was by a wide margin the wettest day in a series from 1891.
The Midlands provisionally recorded its wettest 3-day period on record.

sourceRecords.title: Further rainfall and flooding across north of the UK

dry-then-deluge.name: Dry weather followed by an abrupt return to heavy rain
dry-then-deluge.summary: A drought ends with heavy rain. Hard, dry ground can shed intense rain quickly, so surface-water flooding can occur while rivers and groundwater are still low.
body: The record wet April to July 2012 abruptly ended the 2010–2012 drought. After the dry summer and autumn of 2003, 20–23 November brought double the November average in parts of south-east England. Drought and flood are not opposites in time: the same year can bring both.
regions: Most drought-prone, then exposed to heavy rain.

essential: A drought or long dry spell.
A sudden switch to heavy rain.

outcomes: Surface-water flooding on dry, hard ground.

events.title: Warm, dry and sunny 2003
events.summary: The warmest year in the UK series at the time; August and September were exceptionally dry in many areas, and November brought double the average in parts of the south-east after a dry summer and autumn.
observations: UK 2003: warmest, third driest and second sunniest year in the series from 1961.

events.title: England and Wales drought 2010–2012
events.summary: A sequence of dry months, especially in spring, autumn and winter. One of the ten most significant one-to-two-year droughts for England and Wales in a century; hosepipe bans for six million people in north-west England in 2010. Ended abruptly by the record rain of April–July 2012.
observations: April 2010 to March 2012: equal-driest two-year period for southern England in records from 1910.

events.title: Record rainfall, April to July 2012
events.summary: A shift of the jet stream to a much more southerly track than normal sent a succession of lows across the southern half of the UK, abruptly ending the 2010–2012 drought. The far north-west of Scotland stayed much drier than average.
observations: April, June and April–July each the wettest on record in the England & Wales series from 1766.
Summer 2012 the wettest for the UK since 1912.

damaging-windstorm.name: Damaging windstorm
damaging-windstorm.summary: A storm whose gusts are strong enough to bring down trees, damage buildings and cut power over a wide area. The Met Office notes gales are the most common cause of damage and disruption in the UK.
body: Damage depends on the strength of the gusts (brief peaks lasting seconds), how widespread they are, the time of day, and the state of the trees: the Met Office repeatedly notes trees in full leaf or on saturated ground are more vulnerable. Wind direction matters too — Storm Arwen's unusually northerly winds may have added to the toll of felled trees.
Recent examples range from "fairly typical" winter storms (Erik 2019, Otto 2023) to exceptional ones (Eunice 2022, Éowyn 2025).
regions: Less frequent but high impact (dense trees and population).

essential: A deep low with a strong pressure gradient.
favourable: Trees in leaf or saturated ground.

outcomes: Trees down, blocking roads and railways.

impacts.people: Deaths and injuries from falling trees and debris.
impacts.power: Outages for hundreds of thousands to over a million customers in major storms.
impacts.transport: Road, rail, ferry and air disruption.

signals: Gust forecasts and ensemble probabilities
Probability of damaging gusts by location.
Gusts vary hugely with exposure.
Met Office warnings
Impact-based assessment.
damaging-windstorm.frequency: Seasonally common from autumn to early spring.

stats.text: Gales are the most common cause of damage and disruption in the UK; between 1962 and 1995, 184 deaths were caused by building failures resulting from wind (Met Office citing an ABI report).

safety: Secure loose objects such as bins, garden furniture and trampolines before strong winds.
During the storm stay indoors as much as possible; do not walk or shelter close to buildings and trees.
Even from the shore, large breaking waves can sweep you off your feet and out to sea.
After a storm, do not touch electrical or telephone cables that have been blown down.

events.title: The Great Storm of 1987
events.summary: A depression that formed over the Bay of Biscay deepened rapidly and crossed southern England overnight. 18 people were killed in England and about 15 million trees were blown down. Forecast models in the final day suggested the worst would stay over the Channel.
observations: Strongest UK gust 100 knots at Shoreham (Sussex).
Gusts of 70 knots or more for three to four consecutive hours in south-east England.
Central pressure 953 mb over the western Channel at midnight.
Analysis suggested such conditions over land in south and south-east England might be expected on average once in 200 years; over the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland, once every 30 to 40 years.

events.title: Burns' Day Storm
events.summary: An intense depression tracked across southern Scotland in daylight, bringing severe gales and storm-force winds to much of England and Wales. Winds affected a much larger area than in October 1987 and struck during the day, so there were more casualties: 47 lives were lost.
observations: Wind speeds comparable to October 1987, and higher over parts of southern England and Wales.
47 deaths.

events.title: Strong winds, 27 October 2002
events.summary: Gales and severe gales across the south of the UK as a low moved rapidly across the country to Denmark.
observations: Highest hourly mean 68 knots (78 mph) at the Needles.

events.title: January 2005 stormy spells
events.summary: Two stormy spells in the first half of the month. Northern England took a battering on the 7th and 8th: lorries overturned and 80,000 customers lost power in north-east England.
observations: Many wind-speed records were set during the month.

events.title: Winter storm, 3 January 2012
events.summary: The Central Belt's most severe storm for 13 years (since 26 December 1998), part of a turbulent spell from late November.
observations: Gusts well over 70 knots (81 mph) in southern Scotland.

events.title: Autumn storm, 28 October 2013
events.summary: A fast-moving, vigorous depression. Most damage came from trees still in full leaf. Four people were killed and commuter rail was suspended. Judged within the top ten autumn storms for southern England in 40 years, but not in the same category as 1987.
observations: Highest gust 86 knots (99 mph) at Needles Old Battery.
Gusts 60 to 70 knots (69 to 81 mph) across south-east England.

events.title: Storm Arwen
events.summary: A red warning for wind was issued as a developing storm tracked south to the north-east of the UK, bringing damaging NORTHERLY winds. The unusual wind direction may have contributed to the number of trees felled. Three people died and more than a million homes lost power, over 100,000 for several days.
observations: Highest gust 85 knots (98 mph) at Brizlee Wood, Northumberland.
Northerly gusts widely over 60 knots (69 mph).

events.title: Storms Malik and Corrie
events.summary: Two storms 36 hours apart brought damaging north-westerly winds. Two people were killed by falling trees.
observations: Corrie: 80 knots (92 mph) at Stornoway Airport; 79 knots at Inverbervie.

events.title: Storms Dudley, Eunice and Franklin
events.summary: Three named storms in a week, the first time since naming began in 2015/16. Eunice brought two rare red warnings and was the most severe and damaging storm to affect England and Wales since February 2014. Four people died in the UK and Ireland from falling trees and over a million homes lost power.
observations: Gust of 106 knots (122 mph) at Needles Old Battery, Isle of Wight — a new England gust record.
Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) widely across southern England.
Severe coastal flooding in the Severn Estuary avoided: the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in places.

events.title: Storms Isha and Jocelyn
events.summary: Two storms in quick succession driven by a powerful jet stream, itself intensified by a large temperature contrast across North America. Isha brought an amber warning over more than half the UK and an overnight red warning for north-east Scotland.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) in Northumberland.
Most significant widespread wind storm since Eunice in February 2022.

events.title: Storm Darragh
events.summary: A red warning for wind covered West Wales and both coasts of the Bristol Channel. Two weeks after storm Bert, a further 50 to 100 mm fell over upland Wales.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots or higher in the red-warning area.
Broadly comparable with Isha, slightly less severe than Eunice; 12 February 2014 was much more severe.

events.title: Storm Éowyn
events.summary: The UK's most powerful wind storm for over a decade and, for Northern Ireland, the most significant since the Boxing Day Storm of 1998. A red warning covered all of Northern Ireland and Scotland's Central Belt; the public were advised to stay at home and schools closed.
observations: Highest gust 87 knots (100 mph) at Drumalbin, Lanarkshire.
Tiree recorded the UK's lowest pressure since storm naming began in autumn 2015.

events.title: Storm Amy
events.summary: An unusually severe, though not unprecedented, October storm for Scotland and Northern Ireland, with heavy rain on top of the wind.
observations: Gusts over 80 knots (92 mph) at the most exposed sites.
100 to 150 mm of rain on western and northern uplands in the first four days of October.

events.title: Storm Goretti
events.summary: A multi-hazard storm: damaging winds in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, and widespread lying snow on its northern flank across much of Wales, parts of the West Midlands and the South Pennines. One of the most impactful storms in the far south-west in recent decades.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) at St Mary's Airport — the highest on the Isles of Scilly for 47 years.

events.title: Storm Dave
events.summary: The most severe April windstorm since storm naming began in autumn 2015, judged by the number of stations exceeding 50 and 60 knots. The most severe April windstorm in the observational record remains 1 April 1994.
observations: Gust of 81 knots (93 mph) at Capel Curig — its highest April gust in a 30-year record.
UK April gust record: 87 knots (100 mph) at Flat Holm, 1 April 1994.

exceptional-windstorm.name: Rare, exceptionally damaging windstorm
exceptional-windstorm.summary: A storm in a different league from the usual winter gales — the Great Storm of 1987, the Burns' Day Storm of 1990, Eunice in 2022, Éowyn in 2025.
body: The Met Office's analysis of 1987 suggested such extreme conditions over land in south and south-east England might be expected on average once in 200 years, but that over the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland winds as strong could be expected once every 30 to 40 years — "exceptional" is relative to place. The Burns' Day Storm (25 January 1990) struck in daylight over a much larger area and killed 47 people.
Éowyn (24 January 2025) was described as the UK's most powerful wind storm for over a decade, and for Northern Ireland the most significant since the Boxing Day Storm of 1998.
regions: Strong winds are far more frequent here, so the threshold for "exceptional" is higher.

essential: An exceptionally intense, often explosively deepening low.

outcomes: Widespread destruction of trees and buildings.
signals: Red warnings
Issued when danger to life is likely.
exceptional-windstorm.frequency: Rare; the Met Office return-period estimate for 1987-strength winds over south-east England is about once in 200 years.

stats.text: 1987-strength winds: about once in 200 years over land in south and south-east England; once every 30–40 years over the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland.

sting-jet.name: Sting jet
sting-jet.summary: A narrow core of extreme winds — often 100 mph or more — that descends from the cloud head of a rapidly deepening low for a few hours. The Great Storm of 1987 is the classic example.
body: The Met Office describes the sting jet as a small area of very intense winds, often about 30 miles across, lasting only 3 to 4 hours. It starts 3–4 km above the ground; snow and rain falling into it evaporate and cool it, so it accelerates as it descends — "like a rollercoaster taking the first drop".
On satellite imagery the end of the cold conveyor forms a hooked cloud with a point at its end — like the sting in a scorpion's tail. Water-vapour imagery may show dark fingers of very dry air.
regions: Can occur wherever an explosively deepening low tracks.

essential: A rapidly deepening low with a cloud head.

outcomes: Short-lived, extreme, localised gusts behind the low centre.
signals: Satellite hooked cloud head

Small size makes forecasting difficult.

widespread-gales.name: Widespread gale-force winds
widespread-gales.summary: Strong sustained winds over a large area, not just exposed coasts. Note the difference: a gale refers to mean wind speed (Beaufort force 8, 34–40 knots), while damage is mostly done by gusts.
body: The Met Office case study of 1987 explains the distinction: hurricane force on the Beaufort scale is a wind of 64 knots or more sustained over at least 10 minutes; gusts, which are short-lived but cause much of the destruction, are not counted. Even during the Great Storm, the London Weather Centre's mean wind never exceeded 44 knots, while its gusts reached 82 knots.
Inland gusts during widespread gales typically reach 50–60 mph, with 70 mph or more on exposed coasts and hills.

essential: A strong pressure gradient over much of the UK.

outcomes: Disruption to transport, especially high-sided vehicles.
safety: Secure loose objects such as bins, garden furniture and trampolines before strong winds.

events.title: Storm Ciara
events.summary: The most significant storm for gust speeds across England and Wales overall since 12 February 2014, with persistent heavy rain over the uplands of north-west England. The Humber Bridge closed for only the second time in its history.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots widely across England and Wales.
Over a month's rain in about 18 hours in parts of West Yorkshire.

localised-severe-gusts.name: Localised severe gusts
localised-severe-gusts.summary: Gusts far stronger than the general wind in a small area — from a squall, a thunderstorm outflow, a sting jet, a narrow cold front, or terrain funnelling.
body: Gusts can be very local: the Met Office notes lenticular wave clouds can mark places with very strong gusty winds while air only a few hundred metres away is still. Storm damage patterns in south-east England in 1987 suggested whirlwinds accompanied the storm, with considerable local variation in destruction.

essential: A mechanism that brings fast-moving air down to the surface locally.

safety: Secure loose objects such as bins, garden furniture and trampolines before strong winds.
During the storm stay indoors as much as possible; do not walk or shelter close to buildings and trees.
Even from the shore, large breaking waves can sweep you off your feet and out to sea.

outflow-boundaries.name: Thunderstorm outflow boundaries
outflow-boundaries.summary: Cold air sinking out of a thunderstorm spreads along the ground as a mini cold front — a gust front — bringing a sudden squall and temperature drop, and often triggering new storms.
body: The Met Office explains that when a cold downdraught from a cumulonimbus reaches the ground it spreads rapidly, pushing warm, moist air upwards; condensing, this can form shelf or roll clouds (arcus) associated with strong gusty winds, heavy rain or hail. These boundaries can trigger fresh storms where they meet other boundaries or sea breezes.
outcomes: Sudden gusty squall and temperature drop ahead of the rain.
safety: Seek shelter when a storm approaches.

sourceRecords.title: Stay safe in thunder and lightning

post-frontal-squalls.name: Post-frontal squalls
post-frontal-squalls.summary: In the cold air behind a storm's cold front, heavy showers bring sudden, strong gusts, hail and sometimes thunder — often hitting western coasts hardest.
body: After the cold front passes, unstable polar maritime air builds showers whose downdraughts bring momentum from aloft to the surface. Gusts in squalls can briefly exceed those of the storm itself.

essential: Unstable air behind a cold front.

cold-front-winds.name: Strong winds on a sharp cold front
cold-front-winds.summary: A sharp cold front can carry a narrow line of intense rain with a sudden wind shift and damaging gusts. Weak tornadoes sometimes form along it.
body: Sometimes a cold front organises into a narrow band only a few kilometres wide but hundreds long, along which rain falls at torrential rates for a few minutes and the wind veers abruptly. In November 2010 a line of intense rainfall gave 40 mm or more in two hours in parts of Cornwall; during Storm Gerrit (December 2023) intense rain over the south Pennines accompanied a mini-tornado at Stalybridge.

essential: A sharp cold front with strong low-level winds.

signals: Radar
Shows the narrow line and any breaks or kinks (where tornadoes favour).
Nowcast only.

events.title: Cornwall floods
events.summary: A line of intense rain developed with a deep autumn low, flooding St Blazey, St Austell, Mevagissey and Lostwithiel. More than 100 properties flooded and the main line to Penzance closed.

events.title: Stalybridge tornado (Storm Gerrit)
events.summary: During Storm Gerrit, a mini-tornado damaged around a hundred homes in Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, and a major incident was declared. The storm also brought heavy Highland snow.
observations: Intense rain over the south Pennines on radar an hour earlier.

sourceRecords.title: Heavy rainfall and flooding in Cornwall, November 2010

coastal-wind-acceleration.name: Coastal wind acceleration
coastal-wind-acceleration.summary: Winds accelerate around headlands and along exposed coasts, where friction is low, so coastal stations record far higher gusts than inland.
body: Sites such as Needles Old Battery (Isle of Wight), Aberdaron (Gwynedd), Capel Curig (Snowdonia) and Berry Head (Devon) feature again and again in Met Office storm reports because of their exposure. Storm Hannah (2019) brought gusts over 69 mph to exposed west Wales; on 2 November 2019 Needles Old Battery recorded 109 mph.

events.title: Strong winds, 2 November 2019
events.summary: A low brought very strong winds to south Wales and the English south coast. A woman was killed by a falling tree in Dorset.

mountain-waves-downslope.name: Mountain waves and downslope windstorms
mountain-waves-downslope.summary: Stable air flowing over a ridge sets up standing waves in its lee. These can bring strong gusts down the slopes — the Helm Wind of Cross Fell is the UK's only named wind.
body: The Met Office explains lee waves form in stable air, often with an inversion just above a long ridge, when wind blows roughly at right angles to it; the oscillation can bring stronger winds aloft down to the surface as strong lee-slope winds. Rotors — turbulent rotating winds beneath wave crests — are a hazard to aircraft.

The Helm Wind is a strong north-easterly hitting the south-west slopes of Cross Fell in Cumbria, most common in late winter and spring; a heavy cloud bank (the "helm") sits on the fell and a roll of cloud (the "helm bar") lies parallel downwind.
regions: Cross Fell and the Eden valley (Helm Wind).

essential: Strong wind roughly perpendicular to a ridge.

mountain-waves-downslope.frequency: Common where topography suits; the Helm Wind is most common in late winter and spring.

events.title: Early winter storms, late 2011
