coastal-gales.name: Coastal gales and large waves
aka: storm surges and large coastal waves
coastal-gales.summary: Gales over the sea build large waves that batter exposed coasts, overtop defences and make seafronts deadly.
body: Met Office storm reports routinely record large waves battering exposed coastlines: in February 2014 a storm destroyed the sea wall supporting the railway at Dawlish; huge waves struck Porthleven in Cornwall. In October 2020, waves affected south-coast places exposed to the east, such as Swanage. The advice is to stay away: even from the shore, breaking waves can sweep people off their feet.

essential: Strong onshore winds over a long fetch.

storm-surge.name: Storm surge
storm-surge.summary: A rise in sea level caused by a storm — mainly wind piling water against the coast, plus about 1 cm for every millibar fall in pressure. Dangerous when it coincides with high tide.
body: The Met Office explains the main cause is high winds pushing seawater towards the coast; low pressure adds roughly 1 cm per millibar (the inverse barometer effect). In the UK's large tides, timing is critical. On 31 January 1953 a North Sea surge coinciding with a high spring tide killed over 2,500 people around the North Sea, including 307 in England and 19 in Scotland; defences such as the Thames Barrier followed. On 5 December 2013 a surge 2 m above predicted high water coincided with high tide on the east coast.
A negative surge can also occur when wind blows water away from the coast, which can strand ships.
regions: North Wales and the Severn estuary.
outcomes: Coastal flooding if combined with high tide and waves.
signals: Surge model forecasts with tide predictions
Give total water level.
Wave overtopping adds local uncertainty.
storm-surge.frequency: Common in winter storms; dangerous coincidences with high tide are uncommon.
safety: Check coastal flood warnings and keep away from seafronts.

events.title: The 1953 North Sea flood

As rain accumulated, concern shifted from wind to flooding — the Somerset Levels were under water for much of the winter and the Thames flooded through Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Surrey. airmass-thunderstorms.name: Ordinary (air-mass) thunderstorms
airmass-thunderstorms.summary: A single cumulonimbus grows on a warm afternoon, rains heavily with thunder for 30–60 minutes, then collapses as its own downdraught cuts off its supply of warm air.
body: Thunderstorms need three ingredients: moisture, instability (warm air beneath much colder air, measured by CAPE), and something to lift the air (heating, a front, a convergence line or hills). Organised, longer-lived storms additionally need vertical wind shear. CIN (convective inhibition) measures the "lid" that must be overcome first.

In weak wind shear, a storm's rain-cooled downdraught falls back through its own updraught and kills it, so ordinary storms are short-lived. They can still produce lightning, heavy rain and small hail. The Met Office notes thunderstorms can occur at any time of year in the UK but the most severe usually happen in summer, and that they are most common over the East Midlands and the south-east.

isolated-thunderstorms.name: Isolated thunderstorms

elevated-thunderstorms.name: Elevated thunderstorms

Because their inflow is above the surface, elevated storms are less likely to produce tornadoes or strong surface gusts, but can give frequent lightning, hail and heavy rain.

supercells.name: Supercell thunderstorms
supercells.summary: A thunderstorm with a persistent, deep rotating updraught (a mesocyclone). Supercells are possible in the UK but much less routine than ordinary storms; they need strong vertical wind shear as well as instability.
body: The Met Office explains that in strong vertical wind shear a thunderstorm updraught may begin to rotate: shear creates horizontal spin which the updraught tilts into the vertical. Thunderstorms with persistent, deep rotation are called supercells. They can produce large hail, damaging winds and, more rarely, tornadoes.

Important caveat: a hot or humid day does not make a supercell environment. UK supercells need the uncommon combination of enough instability AND strong shear, often in late spring and summer plume setups or with vigorous troughs. High CAPE with weak shear produces ordinary or multicell storms, not supercells.

capped-environment.name: Thunderstorms suppressed by a strong cap
capped-environment.summary: A warm layer aloft (high CIN) stops surface thermals rising. Instability builds beneath it all day: often nothing happens, but if something breaks the cap, storms can be explosive.

high-cape-storms.name: Thunderstorms in high-CAPE environments
high-cape-storms.summary: Very high instability allows strong updraughts, tall storms, large hail and frequent lightning — if storms initiate. High CAPE alone guarantees nothing.
body: CAPE measures how much energy a rising parcel could gain; it says nothing about whether air will actually rise (CIN and lift) or whether storms will organise (shear). UK CAPE values are modest by continental standards, and very high values usually come with hot, humid plumes.
outcomes: Vigorous storms with hail and lightning.
Or no storms at all if the cap holds.
safety: When you hear thunder you are already within range of the next ground flash; lightning can strike as far as 10 miles from the centre of a storm.

If outside, avoid water and find a low-lying open place a safe distance from trees, poles and metal objects. If exposed, squat close to the ground with hands on knees and head tucked in; do not lie down.
Keep away from underground or low-lying spaces such as car parks, basements and underpasses, which can flood rapidly.

sheared-storms.name: Thunderstorms in strong deep-layer wind shear
sheared-storms.summary: When winds change strongly with height, storms tilt so their downdraught does not choke the updraught. They last longer, organise into lines or supercells, and can rotate.
body: Shear is the key ingredient separating short-lived ordinary storms from organised ones. The Met Office describes how strong vertical wind shear creates horizontal spin that the updraught tilts upright, producing rotating storms. Strong shear is commoner in the cooler half of the year in the UK, when instability is often lacking — which is why organised severe convection here so often needs both to coincide briefly.

essential: Strong change of wind speed/direction with height.

sheared-storms.frequency: Plausible; organised severe storms remain much less routine than ordinary ones.

forced-low-cape.name: Low-instability but strongly forced thunderstorms
forced-low-cape.summary: Little instability, but very strong lift and shear along a vigorous cold front produce a narrow line of intense convection — with damaging gusts and occasional tornadoes — mostly in autumn and winter.
body: A cold front pushing into mild air with a powerful jet overhead can produce line convection with little or no lightning but intense rain and severe gusts. The Stalybridge mini-tornado during Storm Gerrit (December 2023) and the reported tornadoes on 15 October 2002 occurred in strongly forced autumn and winter situations rather than summer heat.
outcomes: Narrow line of torrential rain and squalls.
forced-low-cape.frequency: Common in the cooler half of the year.
safety: Take warnings for wind seriously even in "just a front".

events.title: Stalybridge tornado (Storm Gerrit)
events.summary: During Storm Gerrit, a mini-tornado damaged around a hundred homes in Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, and a major incident was declared. The storm also brought heavy Highland snow.
observations: Intense rain over the south Pennines on radar an hour earlier.

tornadic-storms.name: Tornado-producing thunderstorms
tornadic-storms.summary: A rapidly rotating column of air reaching from a storm cloud to the ground. The Met Office says around 30 tornadoes a year are reported in the UK — typically small and short-lived, but capable of structural damage.
body: The Met Office describes typical tornadoes as 20–100 m wide, lasting a few minutes, with tracks around a mile and winds of 75–100 mph; damage is localised to the track. UK tornadoes come from both supercells and, more often, from non-supercell storms on cold fronts, squall lines and convergence lines. The Met Office notes the UK has little need of tornado warnings and works with NOAA on the science.
Tornadoes are possible in the UK in any month, but they are far less routine than ordinary thunderstorms, and stronger, longer-track tornadoes are rare.

essential: A storm with strong low-level rotation or shear along a boundary.
favourable: Strong low-level shear and storm-relative helicity.

outcomes: Narrow tracks of severe damage to roofs, trees and vehicles.
signals: Low-level shear, helicity, LCL height
Combined ingredients raise tornado potential.
No parameter guarantees a tornado.
Radar velocity couplets
Indicate rotation.
Small UK tornadoes are often below radar resolution.
tornadic-storms.frequency: Around 30 reported per year in the UK (Met Office); individual locations are rarely affected.

events.title: Tornado reports, 15 October 2002
events.summary: A low moving up from the south-west brought heavy rain to southern and eastern England. A tornado was reported in Torbay in the morning and others in Essex later.
observations: Some stations around The Wash had their normal October rainfall in 6 to 12 hours.

events.title: Storm Ciarán
events.summary: An exceptionally severe storm for the time of year. Its track meant northern France and the Channel Islands bore the brunt, with winds comparable to south-east England in October 1987; for the UK, recorded winds were fairly typical of a major Atlantic storm. Intense squally rain bands crossed the Channel Islands with very large hail and a reported tornado in Jersey.
observations: 953.6 hPa at Culdrose and St Catherine's Point, which the Met Office reports as England's lowest November pressure.
Gusts of 60 to 70 knots (69 to 81 mph) on the south coast.

weak-tornadoes.name: Weak tornadoes with showers or convergence lines
weak-tornadoes.summary: Brief, small tornadoes from showers, convergence lines or cold fronts — not supercells. Most UK tornadoes are of this kind.
body: Non-supercell tornadoes form when existing spin near the ground along a boundary is stretched by a developing updraught. The Met Office describes funnel clouds in the UK as often looking like thin dangling ropes; in a typical year the UK sees around 30–35 tornadoes, though it is very rare that they are strong enough to cause significant damage. Exceptions do occur: around a hundred homes were damaged by a mini-tornado in Stalybridge in December 2023.
outcomes: Short damage tracks, roof damage, uprooted trees.
safety: When you hear thunder you are already within range of the next ground flash; lightning can strike as far as 10 miles from the centre of a storm.

organised-tornadoes.name: Stronger, organised tornado-producing storms
organised-tornadoes.summary: Supercell-driven tornadoes with longer, more damaging tracks. Meteorologically possible in the UK when the ingredients align, but rare.
body: The Met Office explains that the most violent tornadoes are rarely seen outside the USA, Canada and Bangladesh. In the UK, stronger tornadoes need an unusual overlap of instability, strong low-level shear and a discrete supercell. MyWeatherUK does not quote a frequency for these because no verified UK climatology is linked here; see TORRO for UK tornado records.

waterspouts.name: Waterspouts around UK coastal waters
waterspouts.summary: A tornado-like vortex over water, most often from showers over seas that are warm relative to the air — typically late summer and autumn.
body: The Met Office explains a funnel cloud that reaches water becomes a waterspout. Over UK waters they are most frequent when cold air crosses warm sea, which peaks from late summer into autumn. Most are weak and dissipate on reaching land, but they are a hazard to boats.
regions: Channel coasts in late summer and autumn.
outcomes: Rarely, coming ashore as weak tornadoes.
waterspouts.frequency: Common in late summer and autumn around coasts; plausible otherwise.

convective-wind-gusts.name: Severe convective wind gusts
convective-wind-gusts.summary: Strong gusts from a storm's downdraught spreading out at the surface, sometimes damaging trees and structures in an otherwise calm day.
body: Rain-cooled, evaporatively cooled air is dense and sinks, spreading out as a gust front. Gusts are strongest when the air below cloud base is dry (more evaporation) or when storms are organised into lines. The Met Office lists sudden gusty winds among thunderstorm hazards.
outcomes: Fallen trees, damaged roofs, overturned tents.
safety: When you hear thunder you are already within range of the next ground flash; lightning can strike as far as 10 miles from the centre of a storm.

downbursts-microbursts.name: Downbursts and microbursts
downbursts-microbursts.summary: A concentrated column of sinking air from a storm hits the ground and spreads out violently. A microburst affects an area under about 4 km across and is a serious aviation hazard.
body: The Met Office notes that virga can on some occasions lead to microbursts: as rain evaporates it removes heat from the air, causing an accelerating sink of colder air and severe turbulence. Damage from a downburst fans outward, unlike the converging pattern of a tornado.

favourable: Evaporation (dry air) or heavy precipitation loading.

lightning-without-heavy-rain.name: Lightning hazards without heavy rain
lightning-without-heavy-rain.summary: Lightning can strike well away from the rain — the Met Office notes strikes up to 10 miles from a storm's centre, and "positive" strikes from the anvil that can travel further.
body: The Met Office explains that positive lightning originates from the positively charged top of a cloud and can shoot out sideways, sometimes travelling more than a mile away from the storm before connecting with the ground — hence "a bolt from the blue". When you hear thunder, you are already within range.
outcomes: Strikes in dry, sunny conditions ahead of or behind storms.
safety: When you hear thunder you are already within range of the next ground flash; lightning can strike as far as 10 miles from the centre of a storm.

heavy-rain-little-lightning.name: High rainfall with relatively little lightning
heavy-rain-little-lightning.summary: Very moist air can produce torrential rain from clouds with weak updraughts and little ice, so there is heavy rain but little or no lightning — a reminder that lightning counts do not measure flood risk.
body: Lightning needs collisions between ice particles in strong updraughts. Clouds in very moist, mildly unstable air can rain extremely efficiently through warm processes without much ice. Line convection on cold fronts in winter often gives torrential rain with little lightning.
outcomes: Heavy rain and local flooding with little thunder.

radiation-fog.name: Radiation fog
radiation-fog.summary: On clear, calm nights the ground cools by radiation and chills the moist air above it to its "fog point". Fog forms by dawn and usually clears as the sun warms the ground.
body: The Met Office lists the ideal conditions: clear skies, light winds and plenty of moisture. Winds must be gentle enough — too light and dew forms instead, too strong and the moisture mixes out. Fog forms most readily near lakes, rivers and reservoirs, and is one of the trickiest phenomena to forecast because it depends on the previous day's maximum, cloud, wind and moisture all at once.
Radiation fog usually clears after sunrise, but in winter, when the sun is weak, it can persist all day.
outcomes: Patchy or widespread fog by dawn.
Freezing fog if temperatures are below zero.
Persistent fog under a winter inversion.

impacts.transport: Road collisions; flight delays.

signals: Fog-point forecasts
Compare forecast minimum with the fog point.
Fog is notoriously hard to forecast.
radiation-fog.frequency: Common from autumn to early spring.

stats.text: Met Office dense fog warnings are issued when visibility is expected to fall below 200 m; severe disruption occurs below 50 m.

safety: Drive very slowly with dipped headlights; full beam reflects off fog. Use fog lights but switch them off when visibility improves.

events.title: The Great Smog
events.summary: Under an anticyclone, radiation fog formed beneath an inversion that trapped smoke from countless coal fires and factories. It cleared on 9 December. The Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 followed.
observations: About 4,000 people known to have died as a result.
Each day: 370 tonnes of sulphur dioxide converted into 800 tonnes of sulphuric acid.

advection-fog.name: Advection fog
aka: fog associated with moist air passing over colder surfaces
advection-fog.summary: Moist, mild air moving over a colder surface — snow, cold ground or cold sea — is chilled from below until fog forms. Unlike radiation fog it can form in a breeze and at any time of day.
body: The Met Office explains advection fog occurs when moist, warm air passes over a colder surface and is cooled; a common example is a warm front passing over snow cover. It is also common at sea when moist tropical air moves over cooler waters, and can drift onto coasts.
regions: Tropical maritime air over cooler sea.
outcomes: Rapid thaw of snow beneath it.
safety: Drive very slowly with dipped headlights; full beam reflects off fog. Use fog lights but switch them off when visibility improves.

sea-fog-haar.name: Coastal sea fog (haar)
aka: fog or low cloud affecting coastal areas
sea-fog-haar.summary: Warm air moving over the cold North Sea forms fog that rolls onto eastern coasts — "haar" in Scotland and north-east England, "sea fret" in parts of England — often while inland areas are hot and sunny.
body: The Met Office notes coastal fog is frequent along the UK's east coast in spring and summer, usually advection fog formed when warm air moves over the cool North Sea towards the coast. With an easterly wind it can cover the coast rapidly; if the land is warm it burns off quickly inland, but if the land is cooler it can linger. In July 2013 easterlies brought low cloud and fog to North Sea coasts while the south and west had almost unbroken sunshine.
regions: Channel and Atlantic sea fog in warm southerlies.

essential: Warm, moist air over a cold sea.

outcomes: Cold, grey coasts; sunshine a few miles inland.
Sudden, disorientating visibility drops on beaches and at sea.

impacts.transport: Shipping and offshore disruption; coastal airports.

sea-fog-haar.frequency: Common in spring and early summer on the east coast.
safety: Sudden coastal fog can disorientate: take care on beaches and at sea.

regionRows.reason: Channel and Atlantic sea fog in warm southerlies.

events.title: Hot, dry spell July 2013
events.summary: High pressure gave almost unbroken sunshine in the south and west, while easterlies brought low cloud and fog to North Sea coasts.
observations: Over 28 °C widely every day from 13 to 19 July in southern England, the Midlands and East Anglia.

valley-fog.name: Valley fog
valley-fog.summary: Cold, dense air drains into valleys at night and fog forms there, often beneath a temperature inversion, while hilltops stay clear and sunny.
body: The Met Office explains valley fog forms where cold, dense air settles into the lower parts of a valley, often under a temperature inversion with warmer air above. Confined by topography, it can last several days in calm winter conditions — producing the "cloud inversion" views prized by hillwalkers.
safety: Drive very slowly with dipped headlights; full beam reflects off fog. Use fog lights but switch them off when visibility improves.

persistent-low-stratus.name: Persistent low stratus
persistent-low-stratus.summary: A sheet of very low cloud covers the hills and lowers visibility for hours or days, under an inversion or in moist maritime air.
body: Low stratus forms when moist air is cooled just enough to condense near the ground but is not cold enough for fog at the surface. It is typical of tropical maritime air in the west, of North Sea air in the east, and of winter anticyclones that trap moisture.

inversion-haze.name: Inversion-related haze
inversion-haze.summary: Tiny dry particles — dust, pollution, sea salt — accumulate under an inversion and give the air a milky, opalescent look and reduced visibility.
body: The Met Office distinguishes haze from fog and mist: haze is a suspension of extremely small dry particles rather than water droplets, invisible individually but giving the air an opalescent appearance. It builds under the stagnant air of anticyclones and in continental air.

trapped-pollution.name: Smoke or pollution trapped beneath an inversion
trapped-pollution.summary: An inversion acts as a lid, so smoke and pollutants emitted near the ground cannot disperse. In fog this becomes smog; the Great Smog of December 1952 killed about 4,000 people.
body: The Met Office case study of the Great Smog describes an anticyclone creating an inversion that trapped smoke from coal fires and factories, plus pollution carried from the continent; radiation fog formed beneath it. The Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 followed, and this kind of smog is now, in the Met Office's words, a thing of the past — though inversions still worsen modern air-quality episodes.
outcomes: Health impacts for people with respiratory conditions.
trapped-pollution.frequency: Pollution episodes under inversions are plausible; smog on the 1952 scale is a historical scenario.

observations: About 4,000 people known to have died as a result.
Each day: 370 tonnes of sulphur dioxide converted into 800 tonnes of sulphuric acid.

ground-frost.name: Patchy ground frost
ground-frost.summary: Surfaces fall below 0 °C even though the air above stays just above freezing — frost on grass and cars but not on roads, and patchy from one street to the next.
body: The Met Office explains surfaces cool faster than the air on clear nights, so a ground frost can occur without an air frost; grass loses heat faster than tarmac, which is why forecasters sometimes talk of a "rural frost". Even patchy cloud prevents it, acting like a blanket.
outcomes: Frost on grass and car windscreens.
ground-frost.frequency: Common in the colder half of the year; possible in late spring and early summer.

precip-visibility.name: Rapid visibility deterioration in precipitation
precip-visibility.summary: Heavy rain, snow or spray cuts visibility suddenly — especially on motorways in spray and in snow showers.
body: Visibility can fall from many kilometres to under 100 m within seconds as a heavy shower or snow squall arrives. On fast roads, spray from vehicles adds to the problem. The Met Office lists decreased visibility among thunderstorm hazards.
safety: Slow down and increase following distance in heavy rain and spray.

post-rain-fog.name: Fog after rain and clearing skies
post-rain-fog.summary: Rain moistens the ground and air; if skies clear and winds drop overnight, fog forms readily because the air is already close to saturation.
body: The Met Office notes that with a high moisture content the temperature does not have to fall as far to reach the fog point. A clearance after a wet day is therefore a classic fog setup, especially as a ridge builds behind a front.
outcomes: Fog patches forming quickly after midnight.
safety: Drive very slowly with dipped headlights; full beam reflects off fog. Use fog lights but switch them off when visibility improves.

persistent-fog-inversion.name: Persistent fog and temperature inversions
persistent-fog-inversion.summary: In late autumn and winter the weak sun cannot burn fog away, and an inversion caps it. Fog — sometimes freezing — can persist all day, and in valleys for several days.
body: The Met Office notes inversions are most common in winter when mist and fog become trapped in the cooler air low down, and that valley fog can last for several days in calm winter conditions. During the Great Smog the sun was too low to burn the fog away.
persistent-fog-inversion.frequency: Common in late autumn and winter anticyclones.
safety: Drive very slowly with dipped headlights; full beam reflects off fog. Use fog lights but switch them off when visibility improves.

dry-spell.name: A dry spell (a few dry days)
dry-spell.summary: Days or a couple of weeks without significant rain. Common and usually harmless — it is not a drought.
body: Dry spells happen in every season under high pressure. They become a concern only if they persist long enough, at the wrong time of year, to create deficits in soil moisture, rivers or groundwater. A run of over 50 dry days at some south-eastern stations in summer 2018 was notable; a dry week in March is not.
regions: Driest region, most frequent dry spells.

essential: High pressure or a jet stream away from the UK.

meteorological-drought.name: Meteorological drought
meteorological-drought.summary: A prolonged period of rainfall well below normal for the time of year — defined by the rain that did not fall, not yet by its effects.
body: Meteorological drought is the first stage: the rain gauge record. Whether it becomes an agricultural drought (soil moisture) or a hydrological drought (rivers, reservoirs and groundwater) depends on its timing, temperature, evaporation and what came before. A dry winter matters most for groundwater; a dry spring and summer most for crops.

For England SE and Central S, November 2004 to July 2006 was the driest equivalent 21-month period since 1932–34; April 2010 to March 2012 was the equal-driest two-year period for southern England in records from 1910.
outcomes: Developing deficits that may lead to agricultural or hydrological drought.
signals: Standardised rainfall anomalies over 3–24 months
Define meteorological drought.
Rainfall alone does not show impacts.
meteorological-drought.frequency: Plausible; most impactful when spanning more than one season.

climate.observed: Droughts have occurred throughout the UK record.
climate.projected: Drier summers are projected on average, though winters are projected to be wetter.
climate.uncertainty: Future drought risk depends on the balance of seasonal changes.

events.title: South-east England dry spell 2004–2006
events.summary: For England SE & Central S: 17 of 21 months had below-average rainfall.
observations: Driest equivalent 21-month period since 1932–34 and third-driest in the series from 1914.

events.title: England and Wales drought 2010–2012
events.summary: A sequence of dry months, especially in spring, autumn and winter. One of the ten most significant one-to-two-year droughts for England and Wales in a century; hosepipe bans for six million people in north-west England in 2010. Ended abruptly by the record rain of April–July 2012.
observations: April 2010 to March 2012: equal-driest two-year period for southern England in records from 1910.

events.title: Summer 2018
events.summary: High pressure dominated June and July: the warmest UK summer since 2006, the driest since 2003 and the sunniest since 1995.
observations: A run of over 50 dry days at some south-eastern stations, lasting until late July.
30 °C exceeded fairly widely on 15 days.
A Met Office study found a summer this hot is about 30 times more likely now than before the industrial revolution.

agricultural-drought.name: Agricultural drought
agricultural-drought.summary: Soils dry out enough to stress crops and grass. It develops in the growing season when evaporation outpaces rainfall, and can occur within weeks of a dry, sunny spell.
body: Agricultural drought is about soil moisture, so it depends on temperature, sunshine and wind as much as on rain. The exceptionally dry spring of 2011 had adverse effects on agriculture; summer 2018 brought widespread drought stress to grass and crops.

essential: Low rainfall in the growing season.

agricultural-drought.frequency: Common in dry summers; plausible in dry springs.

events.title: England and Wales drought 2010–2012

observations: April 2010 to March 2012: equal-driest two-year period for southern England in records from 1910.

events.title: Warm, dry spring 2011
events.summary: The warmest UK spring in 100 years. Rain repeatedly fell in the north-west and failed to reach the south and east.
observations: Parts of Highland Scotland had over 750 mm; some places in East Anglia and Kent had less than 20 mm.

hydrological-drought.name: Hydrological drought
hydrological-drought.summary: Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater fall well below normal. It builds more slowly than agricultural drought and lasts longer, because aquifers need winter rain to recover.
body: Hydrological drought depends on months of deficits, especially dry winters when aquifers would normally recharge. In 2010 low reservoir levels led to hosepipe bans for six million people in north-west England, eased by wet weather in July; across southern England, the 2010–12 drought ended only with the record rainfall of April–July 2012.
regions: Reservoir-dependent: responds quickly to dry spells.

essential: Long-duration rainfall deficits, especially over winter.

outcomes: Low river flows and ecological stress.

winter-blocking-high.name: Winter blocking high
winter-blocking-high.summary: A winter high stalls over or near the UK. Depending on its position and the air trapped beneath it, expect either crisp frost and fog or days of grey gloom — and, if it sits to the north-east, bitter easterlies.
body: Winter highs stop the Atlantic's mild air, so temperatures depend on what the high draws in and how clear the skies are. With dry air: severe frosts, freezing fog. With moist air: anticyclonic gloom. With a Scandinavian position: cold easterlies. The Met Office cites the winter of 1963 as an example of a block that persisted for months.

essential: A persistent high over or near the UK in winter.

outcomes: Frost and fog, or grey gloom.
Poor air quality in still air.

cold-clear-anticyclone.name: Cold, clear winter weather
cold-clear-anticyclone.summary: Dry air under a winter high: bright, crisp days with weak sunshine, and long, clear nights with hard frost.
body: The Met Office notes snow is not the only way to get winter cold: high pressure established across the UK for a long time can let temperatures fall gradually day on day, because the sun is weak and clear skies let heat escape at night.
outcomes: Hard frost; freezing fog in valleys.

graupel.name: Graupel (soft hail)
graupel.summary: Small, white, opaque pellets of rimed ice that bounce and break up on landing — formed when snowflakes collect supercooled droplets in a shower cloud.
body: Graupel forms in convective clouds when supercooled water droplets freeze onto falling snowflakes until the original crystal is hidden. It is softer and more crumbly than hail and is typical of cold-air showers in winter and spring. Collisions between graupel and ice crystals are also central to how thunderstorm clouds become electrically charged.
outcomes: Brief white coverings that can make roads slippery.

hail-showers.name: Hail showers
hail-showers.summary: Showers producing small hailstones, common in cold-air instability. Location and season matter: the Met Office notes hail is most frequent in the west in winter and the east in spring.
body: The Met Office describes three regimes. In western Britain hail is most common in winter, when showers form over the warmer North Atlantic and Irish Sea. In eastern England and south-east Scotland it is most frequent in spring, when the land is warm enough to generate showers but the air still cold enough to freeze droplets. Britain's most damaging hailstorms usually happen in summer, though relatively infrequently, most commonly inland in northern and eastern Britain.

essential: Convective clouds tall enough to freeze droplets.

outcomes: Brief hail, sometimes covering the ground.

events.title: Ottery St Mary hailstorm
events.summary: An unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow forced up over Woodbury Common, produced about two hours of hail. The hailstones were small, but hail banks reached 1.2 m deep and blocked drains; about 100 people were evacuated.
observations: 187 mm in 27 hours at King's School; an estimated 160 mm in three hours (return period over 200 years).

hoar-frost.name: Hoar frost
hoar-frost.summary: Feathery ice crystals grown directly from water vapour on surfaces below 0 °C — the "white frost" on a clear winter morning.
body: The Met Office explains hoar frost forms by the same process as dew but at sub-zero surface temperatures. The feathery kind forms when surfaces reach freezing before dew begins; a more globular "white" frost forms when dew forms first and then freezes. Fog tends to prevent hoar frost by reducing radiational cooling.
outcomes: White frost on grass, cars, trees.

rime-ice.name: Rime ice
rime-ice.summary: Rough white ice built up on the windward side of objects when supercooled fog droplets freeze on contact.
body: The Met Office explains rime forms on vertical surfaces exposed to the wind when supercooled fog droplets drift past and freeze; it is fairly rare at low levels in the UK but more frequent on mountain tops and high ground, where it can build thick feathers of ice on fences and summit cairns.
outcomes: Ice feathers growing into the wind.
rime-ice.frequency: Common on high ground in winter; uncommon at low levels.

diamond-dust.name: Diamond dust
diamond-dust.summary: Tiny ice crystals forming in very cold, clear air near the ground, glittering in sunlight. The Met Office describes it as usually forming below −30 °C, so in the UK it is rare.
body: Diamond dust consists of extremely small ice crystals usually formed near the surface at temperatures below −30 °C; the name comes from the sparkle as light reflects from them. Such temperatures do not occur at UK observing sites (the record minimum is −27.2 °C), so any UK sightings would be in the very coldest, calmest air in Highland glens and are not documented as a regular occurrence.
regions: Only region with temperatures anywhere near cold enough.

essential: Clear, calm air with a little moisture.

outcomes: Glittering crystals in the air; sometimes light pillars and halos.

regionRows.reason: Only region with temperatures anywhere near cold enough.

foehn-effect.name: Föhn and downslope warming
foehn-effect.summary: Air crossing mountains arrives warmer and drier on the lee side. In the UK it gives eastern Scotland and north Wales unseasonable warmth and has set national winter temperature records.
body: The Met Office explains four mechanisms combine: condensation and rainfall on the windward side releasing heat; air drawn down from aloft and compressed; turbulent mixing; and extra solar warming in the clear lee. The most notable UK föhn events occur across the Scottish Highlands when moist westerlies meet high ground on the west coast.
Föhn produced the UK's December record (18.7 °C, Achfary, 2019) and January record (19.9 °C, Achfary, 2024).
regions: Lee of the Highlands (Achfary, Aboyne, Moray Firth).
North Wales coast in southerly flows.

essential: Stable flow across a mountain range.
favourable: Moist windward air (rain on the windward side).

foehn-effect.frequency: Common in the lee of mountains.

regionRows.reason: North Wales coast in southerly flows.

events.title: January warmth at Aboyne
events.summary: Record-equalling January warmth in Aberdeenshire.
observations: 18.3 °C at Aboyne, equalling the then UK January record (Aber, 1958 and 1971).

events.title: December record: föhn in Sutherland
events.summary: A very mild southerly tropical maritime flow crossing the West Highlands warmed by föhn on the lee side, around 02 UTC.
observations: 18.7 °C at Achfary — the UK's highest December temperature on record.

events.title: January record: föhn in the Highlands
events.summary: A localised föhn effect in north-west Scotland. The Met Office notes that föhn is the main cause of highly localised winter temperature extremes in Scotland and Wales, rather than the milder south of England.
observations: 19.9 °C at Achfary — 13.0 °C above its January average and 1.6 °C above the previous UK January record.

lenticular-clouds.name: Mountain wave and lenticular clouds
lenticular-clouds.summary: Smooth, lens-shaped clouds that sit still downwind of hills, formed at the crests of standing waves in stable air.
body: The Met Office describes lenticular clouds as quite unusual in the British Isles but occasionally seen, a visible sign of mountain waves; the waves may exist even without clouds. They can mark places with strong gusty winds and still air a few hundred metres away, and pilots avoid them for turbulence while glider pilots use them to find lift.
outcomes: Stationary lens clouds; possible rotor cloud below.
lenticular-clouds.frequency: Plausible; more often in the cooler half of the year.

virga.name: Virga
virga.summary: Wisps of rain or snow hanging from a cloud base that evaporate before reaching the ground.
body: The Met Office explains virga forms when falling rain or ice passes through dry or warm air. It is usually harmless, but on some occasions can lead to microbursts as evaporation cools the air, which then sinks rapidly — a hazard to aircraft.
regions: Anywhere with a dry lower layer.
outcomes: Streaks under clouds; occasionally gusty downdraughts.

mammatus.name: Mammatus clouds
mammatus.summary: Pouch-like bulges hanging from the underside of a thunderstorm anvil, most striking in low sunlight.
body: The Met Office explains mammatus usually forms on the base of a cumulonimbus anvil as turbulence causes air to descend rapidly, reversing the usual upward growth. Because they form in the most unstable cumulonimbus, hail, heavy rain and lightning may be nearby.
outcomes: Dramatic skies; a sign of a strong storm nearby.

optical-phenomena.name: Rainbows, halos and other optical phenomena
optical-phenomena.summary: Light refracted or reflected by raindrops and ice crystals: rainbows in sunshine and showers, halos and sun dogs in high ice cloud, and rare iridescent nacreous clouds in very cold winter stratospheres.
body: Rainbows need the sun behind you and rain in front, so they are common on showery days. Halos form in thin, high cirrostratus ice cloud and often precede an approaching warm front. The Met Office notes nacreous clouds are usually only visible from the UK when the cold stratospheric polar vortex is displaced over the country, while noctilucent clouds appear on some clear summer nights and are far too high to affect weather.
Included for educational completeness: these are observational phenomena, not hazards.
regions: Nacreous and noctilucent clouds most often seen in the north.

essential: Sunlight or moonlight plus water drops or ice crystals in the right geometry.

temperature-inversion.name: Strong temperature inversions
temperature-inversion.summary: A layer where temperature increases with height, acting as a lid: trapping cold air, fog, low cloud and pollution below, and capping thunderstorms in summer.
body: The Met Office explains inversions often form in high pressure, where sinking air dries and warms, trapping cooler air near the ground. They are most common in winter, when mist and fog become trapped, but can happen all year. On clear nights a surface inversion forms as the ground cools, which is why valleys are colder than hillsides at dawn.
regions: Valleys colder than slopes; cloud inversions.

essential: Subsiding air (high pressure) or strong surface cooling.

outcomes: Fog, frost and gloom trapped low.

events.title: The Great Smog
events.summary: Under an anticyclone, radiation fog formed beneath an inversion that trapped smoke from countless coal fires and factories. It cleared on 9 December. The Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 followed.
observations: About 4,000 people known to have died as a result.
Each day: 370 tonnes of sulphur dioxide converted into 800 tonnes of sulphuric acid.

rapid-pressure-changes.name: Rapid pressure changes with passing weather systems
rapid-pressure-changes.summary: A barometer falling fast signals a deepening or approaching low; a sharp rise follows a cold front. Rates of change say more about wind than the absolute pressure.
body: The Met Office notes that, in general, the lower the pressure within a system the stronger the wind. Very rapid falls accompany explosive cyclogenesis (24 mb or more in 24 hours). Notable lows include 953 mb over the western Channel at midnight in October 1987, and 953.6 hPa in Cornwall and the Isle of Wight during Storm Ciarán — England's lowest November pressure on record.
outcomes: Strengthening winds; sharp clearances after cold fronts.

convergence-zones.name: Sea breezes and convergence boundaries
convergence-zones.summary: Lines where low-level winds meet and air is forced upward, organising showers and storms — in summer from sea breezes, in winter as the snow-shower bands of cold outbreaks.
body: Convergence lines explain why showers so often line up. In late February 2018 the Met Office noted convergence lines through the English Channel and eastern Scotland; persistent heavy snow along one produced a red warning for the Central Belt. In summer, coastal convergence helped trigger the Boscastle storms.
outcomes: Lines of showers, snow or storms.

sourceRecords.title: Snow and low temperatures February to March 2018

exceptional-cold-outbreak.name: Exceptional cold outbreak
exceptional-cold-outbreak.summary: Cold on the scale of 1947, 1963, January 1982, December 1995 or December 2010 — temperatures below −20 °C in places, ice days nationwide, frozen rivers and harbours.
body: The UK's lowest recorded temperature, −27.2 °C, was reached at Braemar in 1895 and 1982 and at Altnaharra in December 1995. England's lowest, −26.1 °C, was at Newport, Shropshire, on 10 January 1982. The Met Office describes 1962–63 as the coldest winter in England and Wales since 1740, with sea water freezing in some harbours.
outcomes: Frozen water bodies and infrastructure failures.

stats.text: UK record low −27.2 °C (Braemar 1895 & 1982; Altnaharra 1995); England −26.1 °C (Newport, Shropshire, 1982); Wales −23.3 °C (Rhayader, 1940); Northern Ireland −18.7 °C (Castlederg, 2010).

climate.observed: Severe cold spells have become less frequent as the UK has warmed.
climate.projected: Cold extremes are projected to become rarer but remain possible.

safety: Check on vulnerable people and protect pipes.

events.title: Winter of 1947 and the March snowmelt floods
events.summary: High pressure over southern Scandinavia set up a pattern that dominated for weeks. Snow fell somewhere in the UK every day for 55 days. When milder air and Atlantic rain arrived in mid-March, meltwater ran off ground still frozen solid, and rivers across England burst their banks; 70% of houses in Selby were flooded.
observations: Drifts up to seven metres deep in Scotland by 12 March.
Woburn fell to −21 °C on 25 February.
Snow depth of 1.65 m near Ruthin in March 1947 — the deepest recorded in an inhabited area of the UK.

events.title: Winter of 1962–63
events.summary: A high north-east of the British Isles from 22 December dragged bitterly cold winds across the country for most of the winter — the coldest in England and Wales since 1740. Snow covered much of England every day until early March; even sea water froze in some harbours.
observations: Braemar −22.2 °C on 18 January 1963.
Blizzard of 29–30 December with drifts up to 6 m in Wales and south-west England.

major-lowland-snowstorm.name: Major lowland snowstorm
major-lowland-snowstorm.summary: Heavy snow of 20 cm or more across populated lowlands, with drifting, bringing the country to a standstill. The Met Office issued two red warnings for snow in early March 2018.
body: Major lowland snowstorms need deep cold air plus a moisture-laden system — classically an Atlantic low running into continental cold (Storm Emma, 2018) or the snowstorms of 1947 and late December 1962. Depths of 16 cm or more were widespread in eastern England on 2 February 2009.

essential: Abundant moisture from a front or sea track.

safety: Plan around snow and keep a winter kit in the car.

events.title: 'Beast from the East' and Storm Emma
events.summary: Daytime temperatures stayed widely below freezing with a strong east wind; snow showers organised along convergence lines and the Met Office issued two red warnings for snow — first for the Central Belt, then when Storm Emma pushed mild, moist air north into the cold air over southern England and south Wales. Freezing rain followed in southern areas. The most significant spell of snow and low temperatures for the UK since December 2010.
observations: Two red warnings for snow.
Cars stranded overnight on roads in Scotland and England; Glasgow airport closed.

sourceRecords.title: Snow and low temperatures February to March 2018
Travelling in heavy snow and ice

ice-storm.name: Widespread ice storm
ice-storm.summary: Prolonged freezing rain accumulating thick glaze on trees and power lines. Common in parts of North America; in the UK freezing rain is rare and true ice storms rarer still.
body: The Met Office explains that ice storms — common in the USA — occur when enough glaze collects on trees or power lines for its weight to break them. In the UK the January 1996 event caused severe icing that disrupted power supplies in South Wales and a 50% rise in hospital admissions in the Birmingham area. Prolonged, damaging ice accumulations of North American scale are not part of the UK record.

essential: A persistent warm layer above sub-zero surface air.

outcomes: Thick glaze; fallen branches and lines.

events.title: Freezing rain
events.summary: After cold easterlies under high pressure to the north and east, a low moved north across southern England. Rain fell through a warm layer into sub-zero air at the surface and glazed everything. Birmingham reported a 50% increase in hospital admissions; severe icing disrupted South Wales power supplies.
observations: A classic "warm nose" profile above freezing surface air.

extreme-short-rainfall.name: Exceptional short-duration rainfall
extreme-short-rainfall.summary: Rainfall totals over minutes to hours far beyond normal: Boscastle 2004, Ottery St Mary 2008, East Wretham 2020, Hawnby 2005.
body: UK short-duration records include 80 mm in 30 minutes (Eskdalemuir, 1953), 92 mm in 60 minutes (Maidenhead, 1901) and 178 mm in 180 minutes (Horncastle, 1960). Met Office case studies give return periods over 200 years for Hawnby (2005) and Ottery St Mary (2008), estimated with the Flood Estimation Handbook method. Impacts depend on where the rain falls: East Wretham's 239.9 mm (2020) caused relatively modest flooding in a rural, low-lying area.

essential: Intense convection that stays over one place.

outcomes: Severe flash flooding where terrain concentrates water.

stats.text: UK short-duration records: 30 min 80 mm; 60 min 92 mm; 90 min 117 mm; 180 min 178 mm.

events.title: Boscastle flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours formed bands aligned with the wind, holding heavy rain over north Cornwall for hours. Coastal wind convergence and high ground triggered the storms and the local topography concentrated the flood. Around 75 mm fell in two hours; two rivers burst their banks and about two billion litres of water rushed through the village. Nobody died, thanks largely to a huge helicopter rescue.
observations: About 75 mm in two hours — the normal August total.
Comparable past events listed by the Met Office: Martinstown 1955 (279.4 mm in 24 h), Lynmouth 1952 (229.5 mm in 24 h).

events.title: North York Moors flash flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours spread from north-west England across North Yorkshire; Helmsley was among the places flooded.
observations: Just over 50 mm in 30 minutes at Hawnby.
Return periods over 200 years for 30-minute, 1-hour and 3-hour totals (Flood Estimation Handbook method).

events.title: Ottery St Mary hailstorm
events.summary: An unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow forced up over Woodbury Common, produced about two hours of hail. The hailstones were small, but hail banks reached 1.2 m deep and blocked drains; about 100 people were evacuated.
observations: 187 mm in 27 hours at King's School; an estimated 160 mm in three hours (return period over 200 years).

events.title: Extreme Norfolk rainfall
events.summary: Thunderstorms gave a remarkable daily total at East Wretham. Flood impacts were relatively modest because the extreme rain was very localised, in a rural, low-lying area — a reminder that rainfall amount and flood impact are not the same thing.
observations: 239.9 mm at East Wretham — a new UK August daily record for an individual station.

supercell-outbreak.name: Rare UK supercell outbreak
supercell-outbreak.summary: Several supercells on the same day — meteorologically possible in the UK when strong shear and substantial instability coincide, but rare.
body: Supercells need strong vertical wind shear and enough instability at the same time. In the UK those ingredients overlap only occasionally, most often in late spring and summer plume setups. MyWeatherUK does not attach a frequency because no verified UK climatology of supercell outbreaks is cited here.
outcomes: Large hail, damaging winds, possible tornadoes in several places.

widespread-severe-convection.name: Unusually widespread severe thunderstorms
widespread-severe-convection.summary: Severe storms over a large part of the country in one episode, with flooding, hail and lightning damage in many places.
body: Successive Spanish plumes from 17 to 21 July 2014 brought 62,277 lightning strikes; during the June 2026 heatwave the Met Office noted extraordinarily high lightning activity, flash flooding in London and the Highlands, and lightning house fires.
outcomes: Widespread flash flooding and lightning damage.

sourceRecords.title: Unprecedented heatwave with high humidity, June 2026

significant-tornado.name: Significant UK tornado event
significant-tornado.summary: A tornado that damages many homes or travels a long track. The Met Office notes UK tornadoes are typically small and short-lived, but can cause structural damage over built-up areas.
body: Around 30 tornadoes are reported each year in the UK, very rarely strong enough to cause significant damage. When one crosses a town — as at Stalybridge in December 2023, where about a hundred homes were damaged and a major incident was declared — impacts can be severe.
regions: Any populated area crossed by a tornado.

essential: Tornado-producing storm over a populated area.

outcomes: Concentrated structural damage along a narrow track.

exceptional-heatwave.name: Exceptional heatwave
exceptional-heatwave.summary: Heat far beyond previous experience: 40.3 °C in July 2022, 38.0 °C in June 2026, 35.1 °C in May 2026.
body: The Met Office called July 2022 a milestone in UK climate history, with 40 °C recorded for the first time and the previous UK record equalled or exceeded at 46 stations. Extreme heat warnings were introduced in 2021; June 2026 saw red heat warnings for three consecutive days.

stats.text: UK maximum 40.3 °C (Coningsby, 19 July 2022); Wales 37.1 °C; Scotland 34.8 °C; Northern Ireland 31.3 °C (2021).

climate.observed: 40 °C was reached for the first time in 2022.
climate.projected: The Met Office says heatwaves of similar intensity to 2018 are projected to become more frequent, perhaps occurring as regularly as every other year by the 2050s.

events.title: 40 °C: the July 2022 heatwave
events.summary: Hot air moved north from the near continent. 40 °C was recorded in the UK for the first time — a milestone in UK climate history — and national records fell in England, Wales and Scotland.
observations: 40.3 °C at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, on 19 July — UK record by 1.6 °C.
Wales 37.1 °C (Hawarden Airport, 18th); Scotland 34.8 °C (Charterhall, 19th).
England's highest daily minimum: 26.8 °C at Shirburn Model Farm on 19 July.

exceptional-warm-nights.name: Unusually warm nights across large areas
exceptional-warm-nights.summary: Nights when temperatures stay above 20 °C — or even 25 °C — over large areas, giving no relief from daytime heat.
body: England's highest daily minimum is 26.8 °C (Shirburn Model Farm, 19 July 2022); Wales's 24.5 °C (Aberporth, the same night). May 2026 brought the first tropical night ever recorded in the UK in May (21.4 °C).

essential: Cloud or urban heat at night.

outcomes: Heat stress with no overnight recovery.

stats.text: Highest daily minimum: England 26.8 °C (2022); Wales 24.5 °C (2022); Scotland 20.9 °C (2019); Northern Ireland 19.6 °C (2001).

events.title: May 2026 late-spring heatwave
events.summary: High pressure and warm continental air brought record-breaking May heat; the Met Office ranks it among the most extreme high-temperature events in the UK record once the time of year is taken into account.
observations: UK May record 35.1 °C at Kew Gardens, beating the old record by over 2 °C.
UK May minimum record 21.4 °C — the first tropical night recorded in May.

heat-drought-compound.name: Compound heat and drought
heat-drought-compound.summary: Heat and drought reinforcing each other: dry soils let the ground heat faster, heat dries soils further, and wildfire and water-supply risks rise together.
body: Summer 2018 combined the warmest UK summer since 2006 with the driest since 2003. 2003 was the UK's warmest year in the series at the time and third driest. Dry soils cannot cool the air through evaporation, so hot spells over drought-stricken land tend to be hotter.

essential: Persistent high pressure through a summer.

outcomes: Heat stress, crop failure, wildfire, water restrictions together.

sourceRecords.title: UK warm, dry and sunny year - 2003

coastal-compound-event.name: Compound wind, rain, surge and high tide
coastal-compound-event.summary: A storm surge, large waves, high spring tides and heavy rain swelling rivers all at once — the worst case for estuaries and low-lying coasts.
body: In January 2014 the Met Office describes strong winds combining with high spring tides and high river flows to produce high water levels and large waves on exposed coasts. In 1953, a surge coinciding with a high spring tide killed over 2,500 people around the North Sea. Eunice (2022) showed how close a call timing can be: the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in the Severn Estuary.
regions: Tidal Thames, protected by the Thames Barrier.
outcomes: Coastal and estuary flooding beyond defences.
coastal-compound-event.frequency: Rare in its most severe form.

regionRows.reason: Tidal Thames, protected by the Thames Barrier.

events.title: The 1953 North Sea flood
events.summary: A storm in the North Sea drove a surge that coincided with a high spring tide. More than 2,500 people died around the North Sea, including 307 in England and 19 in Scotland. Investment in defences such as the Thames Barrier, and in warning systems, followed.
observations: The greatest storm surge on record in the North Sea (Met Office, Storm Arwen report).
About 160,000 hectares of eastern England flooded.

events.title: Winter storms, December 2013 to February 2014
events.summary: A succession of at least 12 major winter storms from mid-December to mid-February: the stormiest period the UK had experienced for at least 20 years. The 5 December storm drove a major North Sea surge. As rain accumulated, concern shifted from wind to flooding — the Somerset Levels were under water for much of the winter and the Thames flooded through Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Surrey. On 5 February the railway at Dawlish was left suspended when its foundations were washed away.
observations: 5 December 2013 surge: 2 m above predicted high water, coinciding with high tide.
Around 6 major storms from late January to mid-February, 2 to 3 days apart.

sourceRecords.title: Storms Dudley, Eunice and Franklin, February 2022

multi-hazard-event.name: Multiple hazards at once
multi-hazard-event.summary: Different hazards in different places at the same time — storms in the north and heat in the south, or wind, flood and snow from one system — stretching response capacity.
body: In August 2020 severe thunderstorms struck north-east Scotland while southern England baked at 34–35 °C; in October 2023 Scotland had record rain while south-east England reached 25 °C. Multi-hazard storms such as Goretti (2026) and Bert (2024) combine wind, rain and snow.

essential: A pattern that produces different extremes in different regions, or one system with several hazards.

sourceRecords.title: Exceptional rainfall in Scotland, 6 to 7 October 2023

prolonged-blocking-anomaly.name: Persistent blocking and prolonged anomalies
prolonged-blocking-anomaly.summary: A block that persists for months, producing record-breaking seasonal anomalies: the summer of 1976, the winter of 1963, the spring of 2025.
body: The Met Office notes blocks can exceptionally persist for months — around mid-summer in 1976 and mid-winter in 1963. Spring 2025 — the warmest, sunniest on record — was dominated by high pressure, with a large anomaly between Scotland and Norway.

essential: A block that repeatedly re-establishes for weeks to months.

outcomes: Record seasonal heat, cold, dryness or sunshine.

events.summary: A high north-east of the British Isles from 22 December dragged bitterly cold winds across the country for most of the winter — the coldest in England and Wales since 1740. Snow covered much of England every day until early March; even sea water froze in some harbours.
observations: Braemar −22.2 °C on 18 January 1963.
Blizzard of 29–30 December with drifts up to 6 m in Wales and south-west England.

regime-whiplash.name: Rapid swing from one extreme to another
regime-whiplash.summary: Record warmth followed within days by severe cold, or drought abruptly ended by flooding.
body: Late March 2021 brought 24.5 °C at Kew; a week later Arctic air gave maximums of 6–7 °C and widespread hard frosts — a fall of about 15 °C. The 2010–12 drought was ended abruptly by the record wet April to July 2012.

essential: A rapid change of circulation regime.

outcomes: Damage to vegetation; stress on infrastructure designed for one regime.

events.title: March warmth then an April plunge, 2021
events.summary: Unusual warmth at the end of March was followed by a cold plunge in early April as a brisk northerly brought Arctic maritime air with wintry showers and widespread hard frosts.
observations: 24.5 °C at Kew on 30 March.
A fall of about 15 °C in a week; several stations had their lowest April temperature for over 40 years.

sourceRecords.title: Extremes of temperature, March and April 2021
